\subsubsection{Green’s function method}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/08_aerodinamica/steady-aerodynamics-2d:green-s-function-method}}

\paragraph{2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional problems}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/08_aerodinamica/steady-aerodynamics-2d:dimensional-problems}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Green’s function.} Green’s function of a 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional Poisson problem reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) = - \frac{1}{2\pi} \ln |\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0| \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Note!} When taking the logarithm of a physical quantity, that quantity must be non\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional. Here, the problem must be made non\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional, as an example scaling all the lengths with a reference length.
\subsubsection*{Derivation of the Green’s function for 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional Poisson problem.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Solutions with spherical symmetry of the Poisson equation in 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional domains, in the whole domain except for the origin of the coordinates (or the position of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{active} point, \(\mathbf{r}_0\), as the problem is independent from translation of coordinates under the assumption of homogeneous domain)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}-\Delta G = \delta(r) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The problem is regular for \(r \ne 0\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}-\Delta G \quad , \quad |\mathbf{r}| \ne 0 \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and it can be solved using the expression of the Laplacian for spherical symmetric scalar fields
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \frac{1}{r} \left( r G'(r) \right)' \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and integrating twice
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  G'(r) & = \frac{A}{r} \\
  G (r) & = A \ln r + B \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The additive constant \(B\) is set to zero, while the constant \(A\) is evalauted by the condition
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}1 = \int_{\Omega} \delta(r) = - \int_{\Omega} \Delta G = - \oint_{\partial \Omega} \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \boldsymbol\nabla G = - \oint_{C_r} \hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{r}} \partial_r G = - \oint_{C_r} \frac{A}{r} = - \int_{\theta=0}^{2\pi} \frac{A}{r} \, r d\theta = - 2 \pi A \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that \(A = -\frac{1}{2 \pi}\), and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) = - \frac{1}{2\pi} \ln |\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0| \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Solution.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  E(\mathbf{r}_0) \phi(\mathbf{r}_0) 
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}\in\Omega} \delta(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_0) \phi(\mathbf{r}) = \\
  & = - \int_{\mathbf{r}\in\Omega} \nabla^2_{\mathbf{r}} G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \phi(\mathbf{r}) = \\
  & = - \int_{\mathbf{r}\in\Omega} \nabla_\mathbf{r} \cdot \left( \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \phi(\mathbf{r}) -  G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)  \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \phi(\mathbf{r}) \right) - \int_{\mathbf{r}\in\Omega} G(\mathbf{r};\mathbf{r}_0) \underbrace{\nabla^2_{\mathbf{r}} \phi(\mathbf{r})}_{=0 \text{ , Poisson eq}} = \\
  & = - \int_{\mathbf{r}\in \partial \Omega} \left\{ \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \phi(\mathbf{r}) -  \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \phi(\mathbf{r}) G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \right\}  \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As shown below, in 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional steady problems there’s no physical wake, i.e. \(\partial \Omega = S_{body} \cup S_{\infty}\), or equivalently on \(S^+_w\)and \(S^-_w\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \hat{\mathbf{n}}^- \cdot \mathbf{u}^- + \hat{\mathbf{n}}^+ \cdot \mathbf{u}^+ = \ ...\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
…

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the perturbation potential, \(\varphi := \phi - \phi_\infty = \phi - \mathbf{U}_\infty \cdot \mathbf{r}\), with \(\varphi|_{S_\infty} = 0\) (\sphinxstylestrong{todo} prove it! And find the trend \(\propto r^{\alpha}\))
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  E(\mathbf{r}_0) \varphi(\mathbf{r}_0) 
  & = - \int_{\mathbf{r}\in \partial \Omega} \left\{ \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \varphi(\mathbf{r}) -  \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \varphi(\mathbf{r}) G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \right\} = \\
  & = - \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S_b} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \varphi(\mathbf{r}) + \int_{\mathbf{r} \in S_b} \underbrace{ \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \nabla \varphi(\mathbf{r})}_{= - \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{U}_\infty \text{ , from b.c.}} G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) + \\
  & \quad - \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S_w} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \underbrace{ \Delta \varphi(\mathbf{r})}_{ = \Delta \varphi_{TE} \text{ , from wake c.} } \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This equation can be recast as an \sphinxstylestrong{integro\sphinxhyphen{}differential equation} for the perturbation potential on the surface of the body \(\mathbf{r}_0 \in S_{b}\) that can be solved by collocation, as an example using \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea/ch/pde/bem.html}{\sphinxstylestrong{boundary element methods}}. Once this problem is solved, the perturbation potential on \(S_b\) is known, and the perturbation potential can be computed in every point of the domain.
\subsubsection*{\protect\(E(\mathbf{r}_0)\protect\)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The term \(E(\mathbf{r}_0)\) comes from the computation of the integral with the Dirac delta.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E(\mathbf{r}_0) = \begin{cases} 1 && \mathbf{r}_0 \in \Omega \\ \frac{1}{2} && \mathbf{r}_0 \in \partial \Omega \\ 0 && \mathbf{r}_0 \notin \Omega \cup \partial \Omega \end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The value \(\frac{1}{2}\) is a particular case indeed, if the point \(\mathbf{r}_0\) is on a locally flat \sphinxhyphen{} no sharp angles \sphinxhyphen{} of the boundary. If the point is at a sharp angle \sphinxhyphen{} being \(\theta\) the angle outside the domain \sphinxhyphen{} \(E(\mathbf{r}_0) = \frac{\theta}{2 \pi}\).
\subsubsection*{Asymptotic behavior of the perturbation velocity}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \(|\mathbf{r}_0| \gg |\mathbf{r}|\), Taylor expansion of the Green’s function \(G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)\) and its gradient \(\boldsymbol\nabla_{\mathbf{r}} G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)\) read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)
 & \simeq G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)|_{\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}} + \mathbf{r} \cdot \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}_0)|_{\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}} = \\
 & = - \frac{1}{2 \pi} \ln |\mathbf{r}_0| + \mathbf{r} \cdot \frac{1}{2 \pi} \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^2} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \boldsymbol\nabla_{\mathbf{r}} G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)
 & \simeq \boldsymbol\nabla_{\mathbf{r}} G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)|_{\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}} + \mathbf{r} \cdot \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}_0)|_{\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}} = \\
 & = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^2} + \frac{1}{2\pi} \left[ - \dfrac{\mathbf{r}}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^2} + 2 \mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{r}_0 \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^4} \right] = \\
 & = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \frac{\mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r}}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^2} + \frac{1}{\pi} \mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{r}_0 \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^4} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
First and second space derivatives of the Green’s function read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  - \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \ln |\mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r}| 
  & = - \mathbf{\hat{x}}_i \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_i} \ln | \mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r} | = \\
  & = - \mathbf{\hat{x}}_i \frac{x_{i} - x_{0,i}}{| \mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r} |^2} = \\
  & = - \frac{\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0}{| \mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r} |^2} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  - \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \frac{\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0}{| \mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r} |^2} 
  & = - \mathbf{\hat{x}}_k \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_k} \left( \mathbf{\hat{x}}_i \frac{x_{i} - x_{0,i}}{| \mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r} |^2} \right) = \\
  & = - \mathbf{\hat{x}}_k \mathbf{\hat{x}}_i \left[ \dfrac{\delta_{ij} |\mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r}|^2 - 2 (x_i - x_{0,i})(x_k - x_{0,k}) }{| \mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r} |^4} \right] = \\ 
  & = - \frac{1}{| \mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r} |^2} \, \mathbb{I} + 2 \frac{(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_{0}) \otimes (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_{0})}{| \mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r} |^4} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Doublet/vortex equivalence}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A continuous distribution of doublets over a surface \(S\) is equivalent to the sum of a surface distribution of vortices over \(S\) and a line distribution of vortices over \(\partial S\). The perturbation potential in \(\mathbf{r}_0 \notin S\) generated by a surface distribution of doublets with intensity \(\mu(\mathbf{r})\) on \(S\) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\varphi(\mathbf{r}_0) = \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \nabla G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Exploiting the properties, \(\nabla G = - \nabla_0 G\), the potential can be recast as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\varphi(\mathbf{r}_0) = - \nabla_0 \cdot \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that the velocity reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{r}_0) 
  & = \nabla_0 \varphi(\mathbf{r}_0) = \\
  & = - \nabla_0 \left( \nabla_0 \cdot \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \right) = \\
  & = - \nabla_0^2 \left( \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \right) - \nabla_0 \times \nabla_0 \times \left( \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \right) = \\ 
  & = - \nabla_0 \times \nabla_0 \times \left( \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \right) = \\ 
  & = - \nabla_0 \times \left( \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \right) = \\ 
  & = \nabla_0 \times \boldsymbol\psi(\mathbf{r}_0) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
having introduced the definition of vector potential \sphinxhyphen{} or stream function \sphinxhyphen{} \(\boldsymbol\psi(\mathbf{r}_0)\), and
having used the vector identity, \(\nabla^2 \mathbf{v} = \nabla ( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} ) - \nabla \times \nabla \times \mathbf{v}\), and the definition of the Green’s function for Poisson equation to see the first integral is identically zero,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \nabla_0^2 \left( \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \right)
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \nabla_0^2 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r})  = \\
  & = - \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \delta(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r})  = \\
  & = \mathbf{0} \ , \quad \text{for $\mathbf{r}_0 \notin S$} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and having exploited the relations \(\nabla \times ( \mathbf{a} f(\mathbf{r}) ) = \mathbf{a} \times \nabla f(\mathbf{r})\), \(\nabla^2 (\mathbf{a} f(\mathbf{r}) = \mathbf{a} \nabla^2 f(\mathbf{r})\), for constant \(\mathbf{a}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The expression of the vector potential can be rearranged using integration by parts (be careful about the domain of the functions, and the differential operators. See below),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol\psi(\mathbf{r}_0) 
  & = - \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) = \\
  & =   \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla   G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) = \\
  & =   \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla \left( G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \right)
      - \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla^s \mu(\mathbf{r} ) \, G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)  = \\
  & =  \oint_{\mathbf{r}\in \partial S} \hat{\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{r}) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \, G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)
      - \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla^s \mu(\mathbf{r} ) \, G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)  = \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that a doublet distribution of intensity \(\mu\) over surface \(S\) is equivalent to the sum of a vortex distribution of intensity \(-\hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla^s \mu(\mathbf{r})\) over surface \(S\) and a vortex distribution of intensity \(\mu(\mathbf{r}) \hat{\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{r})\) over the boundary \(\partial S\) of the surface, being \(\nabla^s \mu(\mathbf{r})\) the \sphinxstyleemphasis{surface gradient}, defined for function on a surface with coordinates \(q^i\), \(i=1:2\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\nabla^s f = \mathbf{b}^i \frac{\partial f}{\partial q^i} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
that can be defined for functions defined not only on the surface as the projection of the gradient on the surface,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\nabla^s = \left( \mathbb{I} - \hat{\mathbf{n}} \otimes \hat{\mathbf{n}} \right) \cdot \nabla \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that \(\nabla^s f = \nabla f - \hat{\mathbf{n}} \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \nabla f \ .\)

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the manipulation of the expression of the vector potential, a \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea/ch/tensor-algebra-calculus/calculus-euclidean.html\#two-useful-lemmas}{vector identity, see the second of the two useful lemmas in vector calculus} is used to transform the first integral, in Cartesian components
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\oint_{\partial S} A t_l = \int_S n_i \varepsilon_{ijk} \partial_j ( A \delta_{kl} ) = \int_S n_i \varepsilon_{ijl} \partial_j A \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or in vector formalism
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\oint_{\partial S} A \hat{\mathbf{t}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_l = \int_S \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \nabla ( A \hat{\mathbf{e}}_l ) = \int_S \hat{\mathbf{n}} \times \nabla A \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_l \ , \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or, without projecting on the constant unit vector \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_l\) the first and the last expressions,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\oint_{\partial S} A \hat{\mathbf{t}} = \int_S \hat{\mathbf{n}} \times \nabla A \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The perturbation velocity is retrieved from the vector potential as \(\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{r}_0) = \nabla_0 \times \boldsymbol\psi(\mathbf{r}_0)\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{u}'(\mathbf{r}_0)
  & = \nabla_0 \times \boldsymbol\psi(\mathbf{r}_0) = \\
  & = \nabla_0 \times \left[ 
       \oint_{\mathbf{r}\in \partial S} \mu(\mathbf{r}) \hat{\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{r}) \, G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)
      - \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla^s \mu(\mathbf{r} ) \, G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)  = \\
    \right] = \\
  & = \oint_{\mathbf{r}\in \partial S} \mu(\mathbf{r}) \hat{\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)
     - \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \left[ \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla^s \mu(\mathbf{r} ) \right] \times \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Zero wake vorticity in steady 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional problems}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As the potential jump across the wake in steady 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional problem is uniform along the wake, \(\mu^w = \Delta \varphi^w\), then \(\nabla^s \mu^w = \mathbf{0}\) and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\boldsymbol\gamma^w = \mathbf{0} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Details in integration by parts on surface in doublet/vortex equivalence}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Using surface coordinates, a surface nabla seamlessly appears}
\subsubsection*{Relationship between doublet/vortex distribution and the circulation \sphinxhyphen{} 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional steady problems}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional steady problems there’s no physical wake \sphinxhyphen{} no velocity discontinuities, zero vorticity intensity, \(\boldsymbol\gamma(\mathbf{r}^w)= \mathbf{0}\). For closed surfaces \(|\partial S_b| = 0\), and thus the velocity field reads (with the unit normal vector pointing into the fluid domain, reversed w.r.t. the original expression at the beginning of this section),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{u}'(\mathbf{r}_0) 
  & =   \int_{\mathbf{r} \in S_b} \boldsymbol\gamma(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) 
      + \int_{\mathbf{r} \in S_b} \sigma(\mathbf{r}_0) \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
having defined vortex intensity \(\boldsymbol\gamma(\mathbf{r}) := - \hat{\mathbf{n}} \times \nabla \mu(\mathbf{r})\), and the source intensity \(\sigma(\mathbf{r}) := \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \nabla \varphi(\mathbf{r})\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Circulation along a line \(\ell_0\) is defined as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Gamma_{\ell_0} = \oint_{\ell_0} \mathbf{u}'(\mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{r}_0) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Focusing on 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional problems, the surface \(S_b\) becomes a line \(\ell_b\). Let’s deal here with closed surfaces: thus the integral over closed surface (line, in 2D) \(\ell_b\) becomes \(\oint_{\ell_b}\). The contribution to circulation of the source term is identically zero, as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \Gamma_{\ell_0}^{\sigma}
 & = \oint_{\mathbf{r}_0 \in \ell_0} \hat{\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \oint_{\mathbf{r} \in \ell_b} \sigma(\mathbf{r}) \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) = \\
 & = \oint_{\mathbf{r} \in \ell_b} \sigma(\mathbf{r}) \oint_{\mathbf{r}_0 \in \ell_0} \hat{\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) = \\
 & = \oint_{\mathbf{r} \in \ell_b} \sigma(\mathbf{r}) \oint_{\mathbf{r}_0 \in \ell_0} d_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) = \\
 & = 0 \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus, the contribution to circulation comes from vortex term only. Manipulating this contribution, it’s possible to get an expression for the circulation as a function of the vortex intensity,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \Gamma_{\ell_0} = \Gamma_{\ell_0}^{\gamma}
  & = \oint_{\mathbf{r}_0 \in \ell_0} \hat{\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \oint_{\mathbf{r} \in \ell_b} \boldsymbol\gamma(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) = \\
  & = - \oint_{\mathbf{r} \in \ell_b} \boldsymbol\gamma(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \oint_{\mathbf{r}_0 \in \ell_0} \hat{\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{r}_0) \times \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) = \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The integral over \(\ell_0\) is equal to \(-\hat{\mathbf{z}}\) (see below), and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Gamma_{\ell_0} = \oint_{\mathbf{r} \in \ell_b} \gamma_z(\mathbf{r}) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{\protect\(\oint_{\mathbf{r}_0 \in \ell_0} \hat{\mathbf{t}}_0 \times \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)\protect\)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Method 1 \sphinxhyphen{} Using Green’s lemma.} In a 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional plane, using Cartesian coordinates, \(\mathbf{r} = x \hat{\mathbf{x}} + y \hat{\mathbf{y}}\), and \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea/ch/multivariable/intro.html\#green-s-lemma}{Green’s lemma} in the plane on a \sphinxstylestrong{simple domain}, the integral becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \oint_{\mathbf{r} \in \ell} \hat{\mathbf{t}} \times \nabla G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)
  & = \hat{\mathbf{z}} \oint_{\mathbf{r} \in \ell} \left\{ t_x \partial_y G - t_y \partial_x G \right\} = && \text{(Green's lemma)} \\
  & = - \hat{\mathbf{z}} \int_{\mathbf{r} \in S_\ell} \left\{ \partial_{yy} G + \partial_{xx} G \right\} = \\
  & = - \hat{\mathbf{z}} \int_{\mathbf{r} \in S_\ell} \nabla^2 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) = \\
  & = 0 \ , 
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
if the singular point \(\mathbf{r}_0\) of \(G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)\) is outside \(S_{\ell}\), as \(-\nabla^2 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) = \delta(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_0)\), and \(\int_{\mathbf{r} \in S_\ell} \delta(\mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r}) f(\mathbf{r}) = E_{S_\ell}(\mathbf{r}_0) f(\mathbf{r}_0)\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
In a \sphinxstylestrong{non\sphinxhyphen{}simply connected domain}, it’s possible to introduce a cut in the domain. If the cut is geometrical and not physical \sphinxhyphen{} i.e. w/o any discontinuity of the functions across it \sphinxhyphen{}, the value of the integral is independent from the path, given a path winding around the hole in the domain the same number of times (\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Add a link to some materia in \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea/intro.html}{(Not so) Mathematics Basics}}),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\oint_{\mathbf{r} \in \ell_1} \hat{\mathbf{t}} \times \nabla G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) = \oint_{\mathbf{r} \in \ell_2} \hat{\mathbf{t}} \times \nabla G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Exploiting this path\sphinxhyphen{}independence, the value of the integral can be evaluated on a circle encolsing \(\mathbf{r}_0\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \oint_{\mathbf{r} \in \ell_1} \hat{\mathbf{t}} \times \nabla G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) 
 & = \oint_{\mathbf{r} \in C} \hat{\mathbf{t}} \times \nabla G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) = \\
 & = \int_{\theta = 0}^{2 \pi} \hat{\boldsymbol\theta} \times \frac{1}{2 \pi} \frac{\hat{\mathbf{r}}}{|\mathbf{r}|} |\mathbf{r}| d \theta = \\
 & = - \hat{\mathbf{z}} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection*{Asymptotic behavior of the perturbation potential}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \(|\mathbf{r}_0| \gg |\mathbf{r}|\), using Taylor expansion of the Green’s function \(G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)\) and its gradient \(\boldsymbol\nabla_{\mathbf{r}} G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)\), the perturbation velocity reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{u}'(\mathbf{r}_0) 
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S_b} \boldsymbol\gamma(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)
      + \int_{\mathbf{r} \in S_b} \sigma(\mathbf{r}) \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) = \\
  & \simeq \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S_b} \boldsymbol\gamma(\mathbf{r}) \times \left[ \frac{1}{2 \pi} \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^2} - \frac{1}{2 \pi} \frac{\mathbf{r}}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^2} + \frac{1}{\pi} \mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{r}_0 \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^4}  \right] + \\ 
   & \quad  + \int_{\mathbf{r} \in S_b} \sigma(\mathbf{r}) \left[ \frac{1}{2 \pi} \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^2} - \frac{1}{2 \pi} \frac{\mathbf{r}}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^2} + \frac{1}{\pi} \mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{r}_0 \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^4}  \right] \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The first term in the second integral is proportional to the mass flux \(\dot{m} = \int_{\mathbf{r} \in S_b} \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \varphi = \int_{\mathbf{r} \in S_b} \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{u}\) across \(S_b\), and so it’s identically zero if \(\dot{m} = 0\), as in the case of solid boundaries. The first term in the first integral is proportional to the «vector» circulation \(\boldsymbol\Gamma = \Gamma \hat{\mathbf{z}} = \oint_{\mathbf{r} \in \partial S_b} \boldsymbol\gamma(\mathbf{r})\) (\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Prove it}), thus the asymptotic behavior of the perturbation velocity as \(|\mathbf{r}_0| \gg |\mathbf{r}|\) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{u}'(\mathbf{r}_0) \simeq
 \frac{1}{2 \pi} \boldsymbol\Gamma \times \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^2} + 
 \frac{1}{2 \pi} \dot{m} \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^2} + O\left( \frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^2} \right)
\end{split}
\end{equation*}



\paragraph{3\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional problems}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/08_aerodinamica/steady-aerodynamics-2d:id1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Green’s function} \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea/ch/pde/bem-poisson-helmholtz-waves.html\#poisson-equation}{Green’s function of a 3\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional Poisson problem} reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) = \frac{1}{4\pi} \frac{1}{|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0|} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Solution}


\subsubsection{Wake and the shape of the domain}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/08_aerodinamica/steady-aerodynamics-2d:wake-and-the-shape-of-the-domain}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Physical conditions, with jump conditions}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{No physical wake in 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional steady flows}
\subsubsection*{Wake in steady 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional flows}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional steady flows there’s no physical wake, i.e. there’s no jump in physical quantities like velocity or pressure across it. Anyways, for lifting bodies, for which \(\Gamma \ne 0\) (see Kutta\sphinxhyphen{}Joukowski theorem), there’s the need to introduce a cut/branch in the domain in order to geta single\sphinxhyphen{}valued potential function \(\varphi\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
…

\sphinxAtStartPar
Evaluating the circulation along a path winding around the airfoil, expressing the perturbation velocity as the gradient of the perturbation potential, a relation between the circulation and the potential jump across the wake is readily found
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Gamma = \oint_{\ell} \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{t}} = \oint_{\ell} \hat{\mathbf{t}} \cdot \nabla \varphi = \int_{w^+}^{w^-} d \varphi = \varphi_{w^+} - \varphi_{w^-} = \Delta \varphi_w \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Theorems}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/08_aerodinamica/steady-aerodynamics-2d:theorems}}

\paragraph{Kutta\sphinxhyphen{}Joukowski theorem}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/08_aerodinamica/steady-aerodynamics-2d:kutta-joukowski-theorem}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional flows.} Circulation along a path \(\gamma\) is defined as the integral
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Gamma = \oint_{\gamma} \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{t}} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let’s define here a circuilation vector \(\boldsymbol\Gamma = \Gamma\hat{\mathbf{z}}\), with \(\hat{\mathbf{z}}\) orthogonal w.r.t. the plane of the 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional flow.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using integral {\hyperref[\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/04_bilanci/04teoria:fluid-mechanics-balances}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{balance equations}}}} of mass and momentum
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \frac{d}{dt} \int_V \rho + \oint_{\partial V} \rho \mathbf{u}^{rel} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = 0 \\
  & \frac{d}{dt} \int_V \rho \mathbf{u} + \oint_{\partial V} \rho \mathbf{u} \mathbf{u}^{rel} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \int_V \rho \mathbf{g} + \oint_{\partial V} \mathbf{t}_{\hat{\mathbf{n}}} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
under the assumptions of steady flow and control volume, \(\frac{d}{dt} \equiv 0\) and \(\mathbf{u}^{rel} = \mathbf{u}\), negligible volume force «\(\mathbf{g} \sim \mathbf{0}\)», and negligible viscous stress, \(\mathbf{t}_{\hat{\mathbf{n}}} = - p \hat{\mathbf{n}}\), and rearranging the surface integrals of stress to get the force \(\mathbf{F}\) acting on solid body \(S_b\), it follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  &  \oint_{\partial V} \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = 0 \\
  &  \oint_{\partial V} \rho \mathbf{u} \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = - \mathbf{F} + \oint_{S_{\infty}} \mathbf{t}_{\hat{\mathbf{n}}} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Details}

\sphinxAtStartPar
…

\sphinxAtStartPar
The velocity field as the sum of the free\sphinxhyphen{}stream velocity and the perturbation velocity,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{U}_{\infty} + \mathbf{u}' = \mathbf{U}_{\infty} + \nabla \varphi \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Under the additional assumption of uniform free\sphinxhyphen{}stream velocity, zero vorticity follows and the second {\hyperref[\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/05_bernoulli/05teoria:fluid-mechanics-bernoulli}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Bernoulli theorem}}}} holds,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  P_{\infty} + \frac{1}{2} \rho U_{\infty}^2 
  & = P + \frac{1}{2} \rho |\mathbf{u}|^2 = \\
  & = P + \frac{1}{2} \rho U_\infty^2 + \rho \mathbf{U}_\infty \cdot \mathbf{u}' + \frac{1}{2} \rho |\mathbf{u}'|^2 \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(P\), \(\mathbf{u}\) the pressure and velocity in any point of the fluid that is reached by a streamline coming from the free\sphinxhyphen{}stream. The expression of the aerodynamic force acting on the body can be recast as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{F}
  & = - \oint_{S_\infty} \rho \mathbf{u} \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} - \oint_{S_\infty} P \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \\
  & = - \underbrace{\oint_{S_\infty} \rho \mathbf{U}_\infty \mathbf{U}_\infty \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}}_{ = \mathbf{0} \ , \ \ \oint_{S} \mathbf{const} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = 0 }
      - \underbrace{\oint_{S_\infty} \rho \mathbf{U}_\infty \mathbf{u}'       \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}}_{ = \mathbf{0} \text{ , from mass balance}}
      - \oint_{S_\infty} \rho \mathbf{u}'       \mathbf{U}_\infty \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}
      - \underbrace{\oint_{S_\infty} \rho \mathbf{u}'       \mathbf{u}'       \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}}_{ \rightarrow \ \mathbf{0} \text{ as } |S_{\infty}| \rightarrow \ \infty }
      - \oint_{S_\infty} P \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \\
  & \simeq - \oint_{S_\infty} \rho \mathbf{u}' \, \mathbf{U}_\infty \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} - \underbrace{\oint_{S_\infty} P_\infty \hat{\mathbf{n}}}_{= \mathbf{0} \ , \ \ \oint_{S} \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \mathbf{0}} + \oint_{S_\infty} \rho \mathbf{U}_\infty \cdot \mathbf{u}' \ \hat{\mathbf{n}} + \underbrace{\oint_{S_\infty} \frac{1}{2} \rho |\mathbf{u}'|^2 \, \hat{\mathbf{n}}}_{ \rightarrow \ \mathbf{0} \text{ as } |S_{\infty}| \rightarrow \ \infty } = \\
  & \simeq - \rho \mathbf{U}_\infty \cdot \oint_{S_\infty} \left( \hat{\mathbf{n}} \, \mathbf{u}' -  \mathbf{u}' \, \hat{\mathbf{n}} \right) = \\
  & = \rho \mathbf{U}_\infty \times \boldsymbol\Gamma \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Circulation in Kutta\sphinxhyphen{}Joukowski theorem}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{U}_\infty \times \boldsymbol\Gamma 
  & = \mathbf{U}_\infty \times \hat{\mathbf{z}} \oint_{S} \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{t}} = \\
  & = \mathbf{U}_\infty \times \hat{\mathbf{z}} \oint_{S} \left( \mathbf{U}_\infty + \mathbf{u}' \right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{t}} = \\
  & = \mathbf{U}_\infty \times \hat{\mathbf{z}} \oint_{S} \mathbf{u}' \cdot \hat{\mathbf{t}} = \\
  & = \mathbf{U}_\infty \times \hat{\mathbf{z}} \oint_{S} \mathbf{u}' \cdot \left( \hat{\mathbf{z}} \times \hat{\mathbf{n}} \right) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using a Cartesian basis, the \(i^{th}\) component of the vector reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \left\{ \mathbf{U}_\infty \times \boldsymbol\Gamma \right\}_i 
  & = \varepsilon_{ijk} U_j \delta_{kz} \oint_{S} u'_l \varepsilon_{lpq} \delta_{zp} n_q = \\
  & = \varepsilon_{ijz} \varepsilon_{qlz} U_j \oint_{S} u'_l n_q = \\
  & = \left( \delta_{iq} \delta_{jl} - \delta_{il} \delta_{jq} \right) U_j \oint_{S} u'_l n_q = \\
  & = U_j \oint_{S} \left( u'_j n_i - n_j u'_i \right) = \\
  & = \left\{ - \mathbf{U}_\infty \cdot \oint_{S} \left( \hat{\mathbf{n}} \, \mathbf{u}' - \mathbf{u}' \hat{\mathbf{n}} \right) \right\}_i \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
having used the properties of the Ricci symbols, \(\varepsilon_{ijk} = \varepsilon_{jki}\), and the identity \(\varepsilon_{ijk} \varepsilon_{ilm} = \delta_{jl} \delta_{km} - \delta_{jm} \delta_{kl}\).


\paragraph{D’Alembert paradox \sphinxhyphen{} 2 dimensional flow}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/08_aerodinamica/steady-aerodynamics-2d:d-alembert-paradox-2-dimensional-flow}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Lift and drag are defined as the components of the aerodynamic force orthogonal and parallel to the free\sphinxhyphen{}stream velocity \(\mathbf{U}_\infty = U_\infty \hat{\mathbf{x}}\). Being \(\mathbf{F}\) the aerodynamic foce acting on the body,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{F} 
  & = \rho \mathbf{U}_\infty \times \boldsymbol\Gamma = \\
  & = \rho \left( U_\infty \hat{\mathbf{x}} \right) \times \left( \Gamma \hat{\mathbf{z}} \right) = \\
  & = - \rho U_\infty \Gamma \hat{\mathbf{y}} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the lift and drag are
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  L & = F_y = - \rho U_{\infty} \Gamma && \text{(Kutta-Joukowski theorem)} \\
  D & = F_x = 0                        && \text{(D'Alembert paradox)} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxstepscope

\subsubsection{Mathematical model}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/08_aerodinamica/steady-aerodynamics-3d:mathematical-model}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/08_aerodinamica/steady-aerodynamics-3d:fluid-mechanics-aerodynamics-steady-3d-laplace}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The governing equations of incompressible flows with negligible viscosity and almost everywhere irrotational can be recast as a Laplace equation, supplemented with the proper boundary conditions. In this model, the thin regions of the space where vorticity is non\sphinxhyphen{}negligible \sphinxhyphen{} namely boundary layers and wakes \sphinxhyphen{} need to be cut\sphinxhyphen{}out from the domain of the mathematical problem: boundary layers coincide with surfaces of solid bodies, while additional cuts must be introduced in the domain to represent wakes. These regions are represented by a (double\sphinxhyphen{}layer of) doublets or \sphinxhyphen{} by the doublet/vortex analogy \sphinxhyphen{} vortices. As shown in the section about {\hyperref[\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/08_aerodinamica/singularities:fluid-mechanics-aerodynamics-singularities}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{singularities in incompressible aerodynamics}}}} \sphinxstylestrong{todo}, the potential is discontinuous across layers of doublets, the normal component of the velocity is continuous (for jump conditions), and the jump in tangential velocity can be related to the intensity of the vortex sheet, \(\Delta \mathbf{u} = - \hat{\mathbf{n}} \times \boldsymbol\gamma\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Let the velocity field be \(\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{r}) = \nabla \phi(\mathbf{r})\) in the regions where the flow is irrotational, the governing equation and the no\sphinxhyphen{}penetration boundary conditions on surface of solid bodies at rest read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 - \Delta \phi & = 0  && \mathbf{r} \in \Omega \\
 \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \boldsymbol\nabla \phi & = 0 && \mathbf{r} \in S_{body} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In order to build a domain where the flow is irrotational, wake regions must be cut from the domain: both sides of these regions become part of the boundary of the domain. In an open domain, the boundary of the domain of the mathematical problem for the kinetic potential is the set union of body boundaries \(S_b\), wakes sides \(S_{w^+}\), \(S_{w^-}\), and a surface at the infinity \(S_{\infty}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\partial \Omega = S_b \cup S_{w^+} \cup S_{w^-} \cup S_{\infty} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Boundary conditions at the {\hyperref[\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/08_aerodinamica/steady-aerodynamics-3d:fluid-mechanics-aerodynamics-steady-3d-wake}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxstylestrong{wakes}}}}} follow from \sphinxstylestrong{jump conditions} of mass and momentum across a wake, the balance of vorticity at trailing edges (\sphinxstylestrong{Kutta condition}) and the \sphinxstylestrong{transport of vorticity}, resulting from Helmholtz’s theorems. Boundary conditions at the boundary \sphinxstylestrong{at the infinity} \(S_{\infty}\) follow from the \sphinxstylestrong{asymptotic behavior} of the fields generated by {\hyperref[\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/08_aerodinamica/singularities:fluid-mechanics-aerodynamics-singularities}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{singularities}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Usually the problem is written in terms of perturbation potential \(\varphi(\mathbf{r})\), separating the effects of bodies and wakes from the free\sphinxhyphen{}stream flow,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{r}) & = \mathbf{U}_{\infty} + \mathbf{u}'(\mathbf{r}) \\
        \phi(\mathbf{r}) & = \mathbf{U}_{\infty} \cdot \mathbf{r} +       \varphi(\mathbf{r}) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that Laplace equation and boundary conditions on \(S_{body}\) read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 - \Delta \varphi & = 0  && \mathbf{r} \in \Omega \\
 \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \boldsymbol\nabla \varphi & = - \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{U}_{\infty} && \mathbf{r} \in S_{body} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Green’s function method, for solving Poisson equations}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/08_aerodinamica/steady-aerodynamics-3d:green-s-function-method-for-solving-poisson-equations}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/08_aerodinamica/steady-aerodynamics-3d:fluid-mechanics-aerodynamics-steady-3d-green-fun}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Poisson equations can be recast as \sphinxstyleemphasis{boundary problem} and solved with a \sphinxstyleemphasis{boundary element method}, e.g. exploiting Green’s function properties. The Green’s function of a 3\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional Poisson problem reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) = \frac{1}{4\pi |\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0|} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that the integral boundary value problems read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  E(\mathbf{r}_0) \varphi(\mathbf{r}_0) & = - \oint_{\partial V} \left\{ \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \nabla G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \varphi(\mathbf{r}) - \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \nabla \varphi(\mathbf{r}) \, G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \right\} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The volume contribution of vorticity field is a function of the vorticity on the body \sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{see wake. Discuss and add details about this statement. For a given shape of the wake, the problem is linear: only the vorticity field, related to the stream function with linear dependence, is unkown; for a free\sphinxhyphen{}wake the problem becomes non\sphinxhyphen{}linear, as the shape of the wake \sphinxhyphen{} i.e. the position of its points \sphinxhyphen{} is unknown: this makes the problem non\sphinxhyphen{}linear, as the shape of the wake is determined by the condition of not\sphinxhyphen{}loaded wake}.
\subsubsection*{\protect\(E(\mathbf{r}_0)\protect\)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The term \(E(\mathbf{r}_0)\) comes from the computation of the integral with the Dirac delta.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E(\mathbf{r}_0) = \begin{cases} 1 && \mathbf{r}_0 \in \Omega \\ \frac{1}{2} && \mathbf{r}_0 \in \partial \Omega \\ 0 && \mathbf{r}_0 \notin \Omega \cup \partial \Omega \end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The value \(\frac{1}{2}\) is a particular case indeed, if the point \(\mathbf{r}_0\) is on a locally flat \sphinxhyphen{} no sharp angles \sphinxhyphen{} of the boundary. If the point is at a sharp angle \sphinxhyphen{} being \(\Theta\) the solid angle outside the domain \sphinxhyphen{} \(E(\mathbf{r}_0) = \frac{\Theta}{4 \pi}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using the boundary conditions on \(S_b\), wake conditions on the \(S_{w^+}\) and \(S_{w^-}\) \sphinxhyphen{} collapsed in a single surface with normal pointing in the same direction of \(S_{w^+}\) \sphinxhyphen{} and asymptotic conditions on \(S_{\infty}\), the problem is recast as an integro\sphinxhyphen{}differential problem with unkown value of the potential \(\varphi(\mathbf{r})\) on%
\begin{footnote}[1]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
What does the value of the potential on a surface doublet mean, when it’s not continuous there? Different equivalent approaches can be used. It’s possible to take a point \((a)\) «just above» the surface, s.t. \(E(\mathbf{r}_0) = 1\) and the singular part of the doublet integral reads \(\frac{1}{2} \varphi(\mathbf{r}_0)\), \((b)\) «just below» the surface s.t. \(E(\mathbf{r}_0) = 0\) and the singular part of the doublet integral reads \(-\frac{1}{2} \varphi(\mathbf{r}_0)\), or \((c)\) «on» the surface s.t. \(E(\mathbf{r}_0) = \frac{1}{2}\) and the singular part of the doublet integral reads \(0\) by regularization.
%
\end{footnote} the surface of the body \(S_b\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & E(\mathbf{r}_0) \varphi(\mathbf{r}_0) + \int_{S_b} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \nabla G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \varphi(\mathbf{r}) = \\
  & = - \int_{S_b} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \mathbf{U}_\infty G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) - \int_{S_w} \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \nabla G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \Delta \varphi_w \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being the contributions on \(S_{\infty}\) equal to zero, and the jump of the potential across the wake a function of the jump at the trailing edge where the vortex line of the wake originates
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\Delta \varphi(\mathbf{r}_w) = \Delta \varphi(\mathbf{r}_{TE}(\mathbf{r}_w)) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Mathematical problem: prescribed wake.} If the shape of the wake is known, the problem can thus be recast as a linear problem
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  E(\mathbf{r}_0) \varphi(\mathbf{r}_0) + \int_{\mathbf{r} \in S_b} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \nabla G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \varphi(\mathbf{r}) + \int_{\mathbf{r}_w \in S_w} \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \nabla G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \Delta \varphi(\mathbf{r}_{TE}(\mathbf{r}_w)) 
  = - \int_{\mathbf{r} \in S_b} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \mathbf{U}_\infty G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or in a discrete form
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left[ \mathbf{E} - \mathbf{D}_{bb} - \mathbf{D}_{bw} \mathbf{T}_{wb} \right] \boldsymbol\varphi_b = \mathbf{S}_{bb} \boldsymbol\sigma_b \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(\mathbf{E}\) a multiple of the identity matrix, \(\mathbf{D}_{bb}\) the matrix containing the influence coefficients of body doublets on body collocation points, \(\mathbf{D}_{bw}\) the matrix containing the IC of the wake doubles on body collocation points, \(\mathbf{T}_{wb}\) the connectivity matrix relating the intensity of  the wake to the jump of potential at the trailing edge, \(\mathbf{S}_{bb}\) the matrix containing the influence coefficients of body sources on body collocation points, with \(\left\{ \boldsymbol\sigma_b \right\}_i = - \hat{\mathbf{n}}_i \cdot \mathbf{U}_\infty\) the intensity of the body sources.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Mathematical problem: free wake.} If the shape of the wake is unkown, the problem above must be supplemented with the conditions of not\sphinxhyphen{}loaded wake \(\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{r}_w) \times \boldsymbol\gamma(\mathbf{r}_w) = \mathbf{0}\). The problem becomes non\sphinxhyphen{}linear, so an iterative method is required.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Note.} The problem is usually solved numerically by collocation. As the intensity of a vortex line \sphinxhyphen{} or a section of the vortex sheed representing the wake \sphinxhyphen{} is determined by a balance of vorticity at the trailing edge, only 2 components of the vector are effectively free. The transport of the wake occurs with the mean velocity \(\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{r}_w)\), and this velocity is aligned with the intensity of the vortex sheet \(\boldsymbol\gamma(\mathbf{r}_w) \parallel \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{r}_w)\). Being the free\sphinxhyphen{}stream velocity \(\mathbf{U}_\infty = U_\infty \hat{\mathbf{x}}\), the shape of the wake can be determined by the coordinates \((y_w, z_w)\) of the points of the wake on different planes with given values of \(x_w\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Once the problem is solved and the potential \(\varphi(\mathbf{r})\) is known on solid surfaces \(\mathbf{r} \in S_b\) \sphinxhyphen{} and the shape of the wake, if unknown \sphinxhyphen{} it’s possible to retrieve the value of the potential and the velocity field in every point \(\mathbf{r}_0\) of the domain,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \varphi(\mathbf{r}_0)
  & = \int_{S_b} \sigma(\mathbf{r}) G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) - \int_{S_b} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \nabla G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \varphi(\mathbf{r}) - \int_{S_w} \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \nabla G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \Delta \varphi_w \\
  \mathbf{u}'(\mathbf{r}_0)
  & = \nabla_0 \varphi(\mathbf{r}_0) = \\
  & = \nabla_0 \left\{ \int_{S_b} \sigma(\mathbf{r}) G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) - \int_{S_b} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \nabla G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \varphi(\mathbf{r}) - \int_{S_w} \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \nabla G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \Delta \varphi_w \right\} = \\
  & = \int_{S_b} \sigma(\mathbf{r}) \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) - \nabla_0 \int_{S_b} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \nabla G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \varphi(\mathbf{r}) - \int_{S_w} \boldsymbol\gamma(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
having used the doublet/vortex analogy, where the line contributions are zero \sphinxhyphen{} \((a)\) contributions at trailing edge of the body and the wake are opposite, \((b)\) intensity of a wake goes to zero at its lateral boundaries, \((c)\) \sphinxstylestrong{todo} what’s the contribution of the starting vortex? is the starting vortex part of the domain? \sphinxstyleemphasis{Discuss}


\subsubsection*{Asymptotic behavior of the Green’s function \sphinxhyphen{} todo: move to section about singularities}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For \(|\mathbf{r}_0| \gg |\mathbf{r}|\), Taylor expansion of the Green’s function \(G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)\) and its gradient \(\boldsymbol\nabla_{\mathbf{r}} G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)\) read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)
 & \simeq G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)|_{\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}} + \mathbf{r} \cdot \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}_0)|_{\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}} = \\
 & = \frac{1}{4 \pi}\frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}_0|} +  \frac{1}{4 \pi} \mathbf{r} \cdot \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^3} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \boldsymbol\nabla_{\mathbf{r}} G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)
 & \simeq \boldsymbol\nabla_{\mathbf{r}} G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)|_{\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}} + \mathbf{r} \cdot \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}_0)|_{\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}} = \\
 & = \frac{1}{4 \pi} \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^3} + \frac{1}{4\pi} \left[ - \dfrac{\mathbf{r}}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^3} + 3 \mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{r}_0 \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^5} \right] = \\
 & = \frac{1}{4 \pi} \frac{\mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r}}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^3} + \frac{3}{4 \pi} \mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{r}_0 \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^5} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
First and second space derivatives of the Green’s function read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} |\mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r}|^{-1} 
  & = \mathbf{\hat{x}}_i \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_i} | \mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r} |^{-1} = \\
  & = - \mathbf{\hat{x}}_i \frac{x_{i} - x_{0,i}}{| \mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r} |^3} = \\
  & = - \frac{\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0}{| \mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r} |^3} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  - \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \frac{\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0}{| \mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r} |^3} 
  & = - \mathbf{\hat{x}}_k \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_k} \left( \mathbf{\hat{x}}_i \frac{x_{i} - x_{0,i}}{| \mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r} |^3} \right) = \\
  & = - \mathbf{\hat{x}}_k \mathbf{\hat{x}}_i \left[ \dfrac{\delta_{ij} |\mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r}|^3 - 3 (x_i - x_{0,i})(x_k - x_{0,k})| \mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r} | }{| \mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r} |^6} \right] = \\ 
  & = - \frac{1}{| \mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r} |^3} \, \mathbb{I} + 3 \frac{(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_{0}) \otimes (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_{0})}{| \mathbf{r}_0 - \mathbf{r} |^5} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Doublet/vortex equivalence}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A continuous distribution of doublets over a surface \(S\) is equivalent to the sum of a surface distribution of vortices over \(S\) and a line distribution of vortices over \(\partial S\). The perturbation potential in \(\mathbf{r}_0 \notin S\) generated by a surface distribution of doublets with intensity \(\mu(\mathbf{r})\) on \(S\) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\varphi(\mathbf{r}_0) = \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \nabla G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Exploiting the properties, \(\nabla G = - \nabla_0 G\), the potential can be recast as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\varphi(\mathbf{r}_0) = - \nabla_0 \cdot \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that the velocity reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{r}_0) 
  & = \nabla_0 \varphi(\mathbf{r}_0) = \\
  & = - \nabla_0 \left( \nabla_0 \cdot \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \right) = \\
  & = - \nabla_0^2 \left( \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \right) - \nabla_0 \times \nabla_0 \times \left( \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \right) = \\ 
  & = - \nabla_0 \times \nabla_0 \times \left( \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \right) = \\ 
  & = - \nabla_0 \times \left( \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \right) = \\ 
  & = \nabla_0 \times \boldsymbol\psi(\mathbf{r}_0) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
having introduced the definition of vector potential \sphinxhyphen{} or stream function \sphinxhyphen{} \(\boldsymbol\psi(\mathbf{r}_0)\), and
having used the vector identity, \(\nabla^2 \mathbf{v} = \nabla ( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} ) - \nabla \times \nabla \times \mathbf{v}\), and the definition of the Green’s function for Poisson equation to see the first integral is identically zero,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \nabla_0^2 \left( \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \right)
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \nabla_0^2 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r})  = \\
  & = - \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \delta(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r})  = \\
  & = \mathbf{0} \ , \quad \text{for $\mathbf{r}_0 \notin S$} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and having exploited the relations \(\nabla \times ( \mathbf{a} f(\mathbf{r}) ) = \mathbf{a} \times \nabla f(\mathbf{r})\), \(\nabla^2 (\mathbf{a} f(\mathbf{r}) = \mathbf{a} \nabla^2 f(\mathbf{r})\), for constant \(\mathbf{a}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The expression of the vector potential can be rearranged using integration by parts (be careful about the domain of the functions, and the differential operators. See below),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol\psi(\mathbf{r}_0) 
  & = - \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) = \\
  & =   \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla   G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) = \\
  & =   \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla \left( G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \right)
      - \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla^s \mu(\mathbf{r} ) \, G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)  = \\
  & =  \oint_{\mathbf{r}\in \partial S} \hat{\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{r}) \, \mu(\mathbf{r}) \, G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)
      - \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla^s \mu(\mathbf{r} ) \, G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)  = \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that a doublet distribution of intensity \(\mu\) over surface \(S\) is equivalent to the sum of a vortex distribution of intensity \(-\hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla^s \mu(\mathbf{r})\) over surface \(S\) and a vortex distribution of intensity \(\mu(\mathbf{r}) \hat{\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{r})\) over the boundary \(\partial S\) of the surface, being \(\nabla^s \mu(\mathbf{r})\) the \sphinxstyleemphasis{surface gradient}, defined for function on a surface with coordinates \(q^i\), \(i=1:2\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\nabla^s f = \mathbf{b}^i \frac{\partial f}{\partial q^i} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
that can be defined for functions defined not only on the surface as the projection of the gradient on the surface,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\nabla^s = \left( \mathbb{I} - \hat{\mathbf{n}} \otimes \hat{\mathbf{n}} \right) \cdot \nabla \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that \(\nabla^s f = \nabla f - \hat{\mathbf{n}} \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \nabla f \ .\)

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the manipulation of the expression of the vector potential, a \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea/ch/tensor-algebra-calculus/calculus-euclidean.html\#two-useful-lemmas}{vector identity, see the second of the two useful lemmas in vector calculus} is used to transform the first integral, in Cartesian components
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\oint_{\partial S} A t_l = \int_S n_i \varepsilon_{ijk} \partial_j ( A \delta_{kl} ) = \int_S n_i \varepsilon_{ijl} \partial_j A \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or in vector formalism
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\oint_{\partial S} A \hat{\mathbf{t}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_l = \int_S \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \nabla ( A \hat{\mathbf{e}}_l ) = \int_S \hat{\mathbf{n}} \times \nabla A \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_l \ , \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or, without projecting on the constant unit vector \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_l\) the first and the last expressions,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\oint_{\partial S} A \hat{\mathbf{t}} = \int_S \hat{\mathbf{n}} \times \nabla A \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The perturbation velocity is retrieved from the vector potential as \(\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{r}_0) = \nabla_0 \times \boldsymbol\psi(\mathbf{r}_0)\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{u}'(\mathbf{r}_0)
  & = \nabla_0 \times \boldsymbol\psi(\mathbf{r}_0) = \\
  & = \nabla_0 \times \left[ 
       \oint_{\mathbf{r}\in \partial S} \mu(\mathbf{r}) \hat{\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{r}) \, G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)
      - \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla^s \mu(\mathbf{r} ) \, G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)  = \\
    \right] = \\
  & = \oint_{\mathbf{r}\in \partial S} \mu(\mathbf{r}) \hat{\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)
     - \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S} \left[ \hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla^s \mu(\mathbf{r} ) \right] \times \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) \ .

\subsubsection*{Asymptotic behavior of the perturbation potential}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Body.} For \(|\mathbf{r}_0| \gg |\mathbf{r}|\), using Taylor expansion of the Green’s function \(G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)\) and its gradient \(\boldsymbol\nabla_{\mathbf{r}} G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)\), the contribution of the body to perturbation velocity reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{u}'_b(\mathbf{r}_0) 
  & = \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S_b} \boldsymbol\gamma(\mathbf{r}) \times \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0)
      + \int_{\mathbf{r} \in S_b} \sigma(\mathbf{r}) \nabla_0 G(\mathbf{r}; \mathbf{r}_0) = \\
  & \simeq \int_{\mathbf{r}\in S_b} \boldsymbol\gamma(\mathbf{r}) \times \left[ \frac{1}{4 \pi} \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^3} - \frac{1}{4 \pi} \frac{\mathbf{r}}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^3} + \frac{3}{4\pi} \mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{r}_0 \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^5}  \right] + \\ 
   & \quad  + \int_{\mathbf{r} \in S_b} \sigma(\mathbf{r}) \left[ \frac{1}{4 \pi} \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^3} - \frac{1}{4 \pi} \frac{\mathbf{r}}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^3} + \frac{3}{4\pi} \mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{r}_0 \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^5}  \right] \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The first term in the second integral is proportional to the mass flux \(\dot{m} = \int_{\mathbf{r} \in S_b} \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \varphi = \int_{\mathbf{r} \in S_b} \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{u}\) across \(S_b\), and so it’s identically zero if \(\dot{m} = 0\), as in the case of solid boundaries.
The asymptotic behavior of the perturbation velocity due to the body as \(|\mathbf{r}_0| \gg |\mathbf{r}|\) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{u}'_b(\mathbf{r}_0) \simeq
 \frac{1}{4 \pi} \boldsymbol\Gamma \times \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^3} + 
 \frac{1}{4 \pi} \dot{m} \frac{\mathbf{r}_0}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^3} + O\left( \frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}_0|^3} \right)
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Wake and the shape of the domain}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/08_aerodinamica/steady-aerodynamics-3d:wake-and-the-shape-of-the-domain}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/08_aerodinamica/steady-aerodynamics-3d:fluid-mechanics-aerodynamics-steady-3d-wake}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Jump conditions.} Jump conditions across the wake read
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
for mass
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left[ \rho u_n^{rel} \right] = 0 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
for momentum, with negligible viscosity so that \(\mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} = - P \hat{\mathbf{n}}\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left[ \rho \mathbf{u} u_n^{rel} + P \hat{\mathbf{n}} \right] = \mathbf{0} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As the wake is (\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Prove or justify}) a contact discontinuity, with no mass flux through it, \(\dot{m} = \rho u_n^{rel} = 0\) (a stricter condition w.r.t. to no jump in mass flux across the surface), the momentum jump condition across the wake reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[ P \hat{\mathbf{n}} ] = 0 \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e. the vector condition contains a non\sphinxhyphen{}trivial 1\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional information, along the normal direction only \(\left[ P \right] = 0\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using second Bernoulli theorem, connecting a pair of points on the two sides of the wake (if needed, do an intermediate step connecting each one of these points with a point at infinity) gives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}P^+ + \frac{1}{2} \rho \left| \mathbf{u}^+ \right|^2 = P^- + \frac{1}{2} \rho \left| \mathbf{u}^- \right|^2 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using the relation between the velocity on each side of the wake, the average velocity, the velocity jump and the intensity of vortex sheet of the wake,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{u}^+ & = \mathbf{u} + \frac{\Delta \mathbf{u}}{2} \\
  \mathbf{u}^- & = \mathbf{u} - \frac{\Delta \mathbf{u}}{2} \\
  \Delta \mathbf{u} & = - \hat{\mathbf{n}} \times \boldsymbol\gamma \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
gives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0 = \left[ P \right] = \\
  & = P^+ - P^- = \\
  & = \frac{1}{2} \rho \left[
    |\mathbf{u}|^2 + \frac{|\Delta \mathbf{u}|^2}{4} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \Delta \mathbf{u}
  - |\mathbf{u}|^2 - \frac{|\Delta \mathbf{u}|^2}{4} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \Delta \mathbf{u}
  \right] = \\
  & = \mathbf{u} \cdot \Delta \mathbf{u} = \\
  & = - \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} \times \boldsymbol\gamma = \\
  & = \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{u} \times \boldsymbol\gamma \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As (\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{discuss}) \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\boldsymbol\gamma\) are everywhere orthogonal to \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\), and thus tangent to the wake surface, it follows that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{u} \times \boldsymbol\gamma = \mathbf{0} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or, equivalently,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\boldsymbol\gamma \parallel \mathbf{u}
\qquad \text{or} \qquad
\begin{aligned}
  \boldsymbol\gamma & = \gamma \, \hat{\mathbf{t}} \\
  \mathbf{u}        & = u \, \hat{\mathbf{t}} \ .
\end{aligned}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Weissinger method}
\label{\detokenize{code/notebooks/weissinger:weissinger-method}}\label{\detokenize{code/notebooks/weissinger::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The present implementation focuses on \sphinxstylestrong{steady flows}, first with prescribed wake and later with free wake. Vortex lattice or panel methods are an extension of Weissinger method, with surface discretization of geometries.

\paragraph{Aerodynamic Influence Coefficients (AIC) and Linear System}
\label{\detokenize{code/notebooks/weissinger:aerodynamic-influence-coefficients-aic-and-linear-system}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
At each control point \(i\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{u}_b(\mathbf{r}_i) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_i = \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{r}_i) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_i \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\mathbf{u}_b\) the velocity of the solid surface, here \(\mathbf{u}_b = \mathbf{0}\) (bodies at rest, w.r.t….), and the flow velocity \(\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{r}_i)\) is the sum of the contributions from the free\sphinxhyphen{}stream velcoity \(\mathbf{u}_{\infty}\) and the induced velocity from vortices with intensity \(\Gamma_j\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{r}_i) = \mathbf{u}_\infty + \sum_j \mathbf{u}_{j,1}(\mathbf{r}_i) \, \Gamma_j \, \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\mathbf{u}_j,1\) the induced velocity in \(\mathbf{r}_i\) from a unit\sphinxhyphen{}intensity vortex \(j\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The linear system thus becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\sum_j \hat{\mathbf{n}}_i \cdot \mathbf{u}_{j,1}(\mathbf{r}_i) \, \Gamma_j = - \hat{\mathbf{n}}_i \cdot \mathbf{u}_\infty \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or formally
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{A} \, \boldsymbol{\Gamma} = \mathbf{b} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sd-font-weight-bold}Exercise 8.1
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Un flusso incomprimibile, irrotazionale, bidimensionale
e stazionario è descritto in coordinate polari dal potenziale cinetico
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
  \phi(r,\theta) = r^{2} cos(2 \theta)
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Si chiede di:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
determinare il campo di velocità, eventuali punti di ristagno,
eventuali linee di corrente rettilinee;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
disegnare le linee di corrente;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
determinare il flusso attraverso il segmento che va dal punto
\(A=(x_A,y_A)=
(0,1)\) al punto \(B=(x_B,y_B)=(1/\sqrt{2},1/\sqrt{2})\) e il
flusso attraverso l’arco di circonferenza centrata nell’origine,
da \(B\) a \(C=(x_C,y_C)=(1,0)\). Discutere il risultato;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
dimostrare che le linee di corrente e le curve di livello del
potenziale sono tra di loro perpendicolari.

\end{itemize}

\end{sphinxuseclass}
\end{sphinxuseclass}

incomprimibili. \$\(\bm{u} = \bm{\nabla} \phi \quad
  \begin{cases}
  \begin{aligned}
   & u_x  =  \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x}  = \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial y} \\
   & u_y  =  \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial y}  = - \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} \ .
  \end{aligned}
  \end{cases}\)\( Flusso di volume come differenza di funzione di corrente
\)\(\begin{aligned}
  \int_{A}^B \bm{u} \cdot {\bm{\hat{n}}} & =
  \int_{A}^B u n_x + v n_y = \\
 & = \int_A^B \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} t_x +
              \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y} t_y = \\
 & = \int_A^B \left[ \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} \dfrac{dx}{ds} +
              \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y} \dfrac{dy}{ds} \right] ds = \\
 & = \int_{A}^B \dfrac{d \psi}{ds} (x(s),y(s)) ds = \psi(B) - \psi(A) \ .
 \end{aligned}\)\$
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Campo di velocità, punto di ristagno e linee di corrente rettilinee
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\phi\), \(\bm{u}\), \(\psi\):
\$\(\phi = r^2 \cos(2\theta) = r^2 ( \cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \theta) = 
        x^2 - y^2\)\( \)\(\begin{cases}
      u = \partial \phi / \partial x = 2x \\
      v = \partial \phi / \partial y = -2y
    \end{cases} \qquad \rightarrow \qquad  \psi(x,y) = 2 x y + C\)\$

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
punto di ristagno: \((x,y)=(0,0)\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Linee di corrente rettilinee: \((x,y) = (0,y)\) entranti
nell’origine, \((x,y) = (x,0)\) uscenti dall’origine.

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
…

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
flusso attraverso \(AB\) e \(BC\). La normale considerata «punta a
destra» mentre viene percorsa la curva: valgono quindi \(n_x = t_y\) e
\(n_y = -t_x\). \$\(\begin{cases}
     \Phi_{AB} = \psi(B) - \psi(A) = 1 - 0 = 1  \\
     \Phi_{BC} = \psi(C) - \psi(B) = 0 - 1 = -1
    \end{cases}\)\( Si consideri la curva chiusa costituita da \)AB\(,
\)BC\( e dagli assi. Non c'è flusso attraverso gli assi e quello che
entra in \)AB\( esce da \)BC\$. \sphinxstyleemphasis{il campo è regolare in tutto il
dominio}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Il gradiente di una funzione è perpendicolare alle curve di livello:
si può quindi verificare che i gradienti siano perpendicolari.
Considerando le relazioni: \$\(\begin{cases}
      u & = \partial \phi / \partial x = \partial \psi / \partial y \\
      v & = \partial \phi / \partial y = - \partial \psi / \partial x
    \end{cases}\)\( Si può scrivere
\)\(\bm{\nabla}\phi \cdot \bm{\nabla}\psi = u v - v u = 0\)\$

\end{itemize}

\chapter{Boundary layer}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/09_bl/09teoria:boundary-layer}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/09_bl/09teoria:fluid-mechanics-bl}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/09_bl/09teoria::doc}}

\section{Equazioni di Prandtl dello strato limite}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/09_bl/09teoria:equazioni-di-prandtl-dello-strato-limite}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/09_bl/09teoria:fluid-mechanics-bl-prandtl-eq}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Steady Navier—Stokes equations for a 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional flow using Cartesian coordinates read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
  u \partial_x u + v \partial_y u - \nu \left( \partial_{xx} u + \partial_{yy} u \right) + \frac{1}{\rho} \partial_x P = 0 \\
  u \partial_x v + v \partial_y v - \nu \left( \partial_{xx} v + \partial_{yy} v \right) + \frac{1}{\rho} \partial_y P = 0 \\
  \partial_x u + \partial_y v = 0
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let’s assume the flow of interest has a main stream\sphinxhyphen{}wise direction, here identified by \(x\) coordinate, while \(y\) runs in the orthogonal direction. Let \(U\), \(V\), \(X\), \(\delta\) be characteristic \(x\)\sphinxhyphen{} and \(y\)\sphinxhyphen{} components of the velocity field and lengths. Non\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional equations become
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
  \frac{U^2}{X} u \partial_x u + \frac{U V}{\delta} v \partial_y u - \frac{\nu U}{X^2} \partial_{xx} u - \frac{\nu U}{\delta^2} \partial_{yy} u + \frac{P}{\rho X} \partial_x P = 0 \\
  \frac{U V}{X} u \partial_x v + \frac{V^2}{\delta} v \partial_y v - \frac{\nu V}{X^2} \partial_{xx} v - \frac{\nu V}{\delta^2} \partial_{yy} v + \frac{P}{\rho \delta} \partial_y P = 0 \\
  \frac{U}{X} \partial_x u + \frac{V}{\delta} \partial_y v = 0
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let the 2 terms in the incompressibility constraint have the same order of magnitude. It follows that \(V \sim \frac{\delta}{X} U\). Using this relation, and assuming \(P \sim \rho U^2\), the non\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional equations become
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
  \frac{U^2}{X} \left[ \left( u \partial_x u + v \partial_y u - \partial_{yy} u + \partial_x P \right) - \left(\frac{\delta}{X}\right)^2 \left( \partial_{xx} u  \right) \right] = 0 \\
  \frac{U^2}{X} \left[ \frac{X}{\delta} \left( \partial_y P \right) + \frac{\delta}{X} \left( u \partial_x v + v \partial_y v - \partial_{yy} v \right) - \left( \frac{\delta}{X} \right)^3 \partial_{xx} v  \right] = 0 \\
  \frac{U}{X} \left(  \partial_x u + \partial_y v \right) = 0 \ ,
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If \(X \gg \delta\) (or equivalently \(U \gg V\)),
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
in the \(x\)\sphinxhyphen{}component of the momentum equation \(\partial_{yy} u\) prevails over \(\partial_{xx} u\); the convective term and the \(x\)\sphinxhyphen{}component of the pressure gradient has the same order of magnitude, given \(P \sim \rho U^2\); the leading contribution of the viscous term has the same order of magnitude if \(\frac{\nu X}{U \delta^2} \sim 1\), and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\delta(x) \sim \left( \frac{\nu x}{U} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} = x \left( \frac{\nu}{x U} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} = x \, \text{Re}_x^{-\frac{1}{2}} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\delta(x) \sim x^{\frac{1}{2}} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In order to have thin boundary layers, \(\delta(x) \ll x\), i.e. viscoisty should be «small enough» to be dominated by convection, except for the \(\nu \partial_{yy} u\) contribution in the thin boundary layer region. Once divided by \(\frac{U^2}{X}\) the leading order of the \(x\)\sphinxhyphen{}component of the momentum equation is \(\sim 1\).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
in the \(y\)\sphinxhyphen{}component of the momentum equation, the leading term is the \(y\)\sphinxhyphen{}component of the pressure gradient, \(\partial_y P\), with order \(\varepsilon^{-1}\), being \(\varepsilon := \frac{\delta}{X}\)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Retaining the leading components of the equations, Navier\sphinxhyphen{}Stokes equation reduces to Prandtl equations, whose non\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional form reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
  u \partial_x u + v \partial_y u - \partial_{yy} u + \partial_x P = 0 \\
  \partial_y P = 0 \\
  \partial_x u + \partial_y v = 0 \ ,
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Discuss the mathematical nature of Prandtl equations (parabolic equation?): which boundary conditions? Examples for different flows: b.l. on flat surface, jet flows, shear layers, wakes behing a body,…}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pressure across boundary layers is approximately constant, as \(\partial_y P = 0\)

\end{itemize}

\section{Self\sphinxhyphen{}similar laminar boundary layer flows}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/09_bl/09teoria:self-similar-laminar-boundary-layer-flows}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/09_bl/09teoria:fluid-mechanics-bl-self-similar}}

\subsection{Boundary layer on flat plate: Blasius solution}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/09_bl/09teoria:boundary-layer-on-flat-plate-blasius-solution}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/09_bl/09teoria:fluid-mechanics-bl-self-similar-blasius}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Boundary conditions read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  u(x=0, y        ) & = U \\
  u(x  , y=0      ) & = 0 \\
  v(x  , y=0      ) & = 0 \\
  u(x  , y=+\infty) & = U \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Assuming irrotational flow outside the b.l., pressure is uniform in the whole domain: as the velocity is uniform in the irrotational region, pressure is uniform there, as a consequence of Bernoulli’s theorems. As pressure is constant across the boundary layer in the orthogonal direction, pressure is uniform both inside and outside the boundary layer, \(P(x,y) = \overline{P}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Without any reference length scale, a self\sphinxhyphen{}similar solution may exist: for a self\sphinxhyphen{}similar flow, fields are function of a self\sphinxhyphen{}similarity coordindate \(\eta(x,y) = \frac{y}{\delta(x)}\) and not of \(x\), \(y\) independently.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using stream\sphinxhyphen{}function \(\psi\), \(u = \psi_{/y}\), \(v = - \psi_{/x}\), incompressibility constraint is identically satisfied. The last equation to deal with is the \(x\)\sphinxhyphen{}component of the momentum equation, that becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\psi_{/y} \psi_{/yx} - \psi_{/x} \psi_{/yy} - \nu \psi_{/yyy} = 0 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(\psi(x,y) = U \delta(x) g\left( \eta(x,y) \right)\), the components of the velocity field becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \frac{u}{U} = \psi_{/y}
    & = \delta(x) g'(\eta) \eta_{/y} = \\
    & = \delta(x) g'(\eta) \frac{1}{\delta(x)} = \\
    & = g'(\eta) \\
  \frac{v}{U} = - \psi_{/x} 
    & = \delta'(x) g(\eta) + \delta(x) g'(\eta) \eta_{/x} = \\
    & = \delta'(x) g(\eta) - \delta(x) g'(\eta) \frac{y \delta'(x)}{\delta^2(x)} = \\
    & = \delta'(x) g(\eta) - \eta g'(\eta) \delta'(x)
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
while all the other derivatives appearing in the \(x\)\sphinxhyphen{}component of the momentum equation read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \psi_{/yy}  & = g''(\eta) \frac{1}{\delta(x)} \\
  \psi_{/yyy} & = g'''(\eta) \frac{1}{\delta^2(x)} \\
  \psi_{/yx}  & = - g''(\eta) \frac{y \delta'(x)}{\delta^2(x)} = - \eta g''(\eta) \frac{\delta'(x)}{\delta(x)} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Inserting these expression in the \(x\)\sphinxhyphen{}component of the momentum equation,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 0 
 & = - U^2 g' g'' \eta \frac{\delta'}{\delta} - \left( \delta' g - \eta g' \delta' \right) g'' \frac{1}{\delta} - \nu U g''' \frac{1}{\delta^2} = \\
 & = - U^2 g  g'' \frac{\delta'}{\delta} - \nu U g''' \frac{1}{\delta^2} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \frac{U \delta'(x) \delta(x)}{\nu} g(\eta) g''(\eta) + g'''(\eta) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In order to get a self\sphinxhyphen{}similar solution, no term depending only on \(x\) or \(y\) may appear in the equation. Thus, the coefficient of the first term must be constant,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}C = \frac{U \delta'(x) \delta(x)}{\nu} = \frac{U}{\nu} \dfrac{d}{dx} \dfrac{\delta^2(x)}{2} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and usually \(C\) is chosen to be \(C = \frac{1}{2}\) (this choice just changes the definition of the arbitrary thickness of the b.l. \(\delta(x)\) by a multiplicative factor. Solving this equation, the arbitrary thickness of the b.l. goes as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\delta(x) - \delta(x_0) = \sqrt{ \frac{\nu}{U} ( x - x_0 ) } \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
while the \(x\)\sphinxhyphen{}component of the momentum equation becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{1}{2} g g'' + g''' = 0 \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
supplied with the boundary conditions
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  g(0) & = 0 \\
  g'(0) & = 0 \\
  g'(+\infty) & = 1 \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
for the b.l. on a flat plate.
\subsubsection*{Proof of the boundary conditions for the b.l on the flat plate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Proof that the 4 boundary conditions written as a function of the velocity field or the stream\sphinxhyphen{}function are equivalent to teh 3 boundary conditions written in terms of the similarity function \(g(\eta)\)

\sphinxAtStartPar
