\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/10teoria:instability-and-turbulence}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/10teoria:fluid-mechanics-turbulence}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/10teoria::doc}}
\sphinxstepscope


\section{RANS and energy equations}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/rans_energy:rans-and-energy-equations}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/rans_energy:fluid-mechanics-turbulence-rans-energy}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/rans_energy::doc}}

\subsection{RANS}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/rans_energy:rans}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/rans_energy:fluid-mechanics-turbulence-rans-energy-rans}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Incompressible Navier—Stokes equations.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
  \partial_t \mathbf{u} + ( \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla ) \mathbf{u} - \nu \Delta \mathbf{u} + \nabla P = \mathbf{0} \\
  \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0 \ ,
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(P = \frac{P}{\overline{\rho}}\) with little abuse of notation, and no volume force. For incompressible flows, the following relation holds
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{u} \otimes \mathbf{u} \right) = ( \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla ) \mathbf{u} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Proof}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using Cartesian coordinates
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\{ \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{u} \otimes \mathbf{u} \right) \right}_i = ( u_j u_i )_{/j} = \underbrace{u_{j/j}}_{=0} u_i + u_j u_{i/j} = \left\{ ( \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla ) \mathbf{u} \right\}_i \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
as \(u_{j/j} = \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0\), for the incompressiblity constraint.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Incompressible Reynolds\sphinxhyphen{}averaged Navier—Stokes equations, RANS.} Applying average operator%
\begin{footnote}[1]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
What’s a proper definition? Can equations be time\sphinxhyphen{}dependent? It looks so, if fields are interpreted as stochastic fields and average is an average in probability and not time.
%
\end{footnote} to NS equations
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\overline{\text{NS}} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
after having defined the relation between the realization of a field, its average and fluctuation,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}f = \overline{f} + f' \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that applying average \(\overline{f'} = 0\), RANS equations follows%
\begin{footnote}[2]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
Is it possible to swap average operator and differential operators? Let’s assume it is.
%
\end{footnote}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
  \partial_t \overline{\mathbf{u}} + ( \overline{\mathbf{u}} \cdot \nabla ) \overline{\mathbf{u}} + \nabla \cdot \overline{\mathbf{u}' \otimes  \mathbf{u}'} - \nu \Delta \overline{\mathbf{u}} + \nabla \overline{P} = \mathbf{0} \\
  \nabla \cdot \overline{\mathbf{u}} = 0 \ ,
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
if average and differential operators swaps for linear terms. An extra\sphinxhyphen{}contribution arises from the non\sphinxhyphen{}linear term, as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \overline{ a b } 
  & = \overline{ (\overline{a}+a') (\overline{b}+b')} = \\
  & = \overline{ \overline{a} \overline{b} } + \underbrace{ \overline{ \overline{a} b' } }_{\overline{a} \overline{b'} = 0} + \underbrace{\overline{ a' \overline{b} }}_{\overline{a'} \overline{b}=0} + \overline{ a' b'} = \\
  & = \overline{a} \overline{b}  + \overline{ a' b'} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This can be interpreted as \sphinxstyleemphasis{extra} stress contribution (as it has the expression of the divergence of a 2\sphinxhyphen{}nd order symmetric tensor) felt by the average fields \(\overline{\mathbf{u}}, \overline{P}\), due to fluctuations \(\mathbf{u}'\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Equation of the fluctuation.} Taking the difference between NS equations and RANS equations, the equation for the fluctuation \(\mathbf{u}' = \mathbf{u} - \overline{\mathbf{u}}\) seamlessly follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
  \partial_t \mathbf{u}' + \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{u} \otimes \mathbf{u}) - \nabla \cdot (\overline{\mathbf{u}} \otimes \overline{\mathbf{u}}) - \nabla \cdot \overline{ (\mathbf{u}' \otimes \mathbf{u}')} -  \nu \Delta \mathbf{u}' + \nabla P' = \mathbf{0} \\
  \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}' = 0 \ ,
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
  \partial_t \mathbf{u}' + \nabla \cdot (\overline{\mathbf{u}} \otimes \mathbf{u}') + \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{u}' \otimes \overline{\mathbf{u}}) + \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{u}' \otimes \mathbf{u}' ) - \nabla \cdot \overline{ (\mathbf{u}' \otimes \mathbf{u}')} -  \nu \Delta \mathbf{u}' + \nabla P' = \mathbf{0} \\
  \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}' = 0 \ ,
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Energy equations}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/rans_energy:energy-equations}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/rans_energy:fluid-mechanics-turbulence-rans-energy-energy}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Here, kinetic energy equation, average kinetic energy, kinetic energy of the average field, kinetic energy of the fluctuation and its average,…
Kinetic energy per unit\sphinxhyphen{}mass is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}K := \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}}{2} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and it can be recast using the average and the fluctuation fields
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 K
 & = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}}{2} = \\
 & = \frac{( \overline{\mathbf{u}} + \mathbf{u}') \cdot (\overline{\mathbf{u}} + \mathbf{u}')}{2} = \\
 & = \frac{\overline{\mathbf{u}} \cdot \overline{\mathbf{u}}}{2} + \frac{\mathbf{u}' \cdot \mathbf{u}'}{2} + \overline{\mathbf{u}} \cdot \mathbf{u}'
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being the first tern the kinetic energy of the average flow, the second term the kinetic energy of the fluctuations, and the last term the cross\sphinxhyphen{}effects. Taking average, to get the average kinetic energy \(\overline{K}\) the last term disappears, and a relation between the average kinetic energy, the energy of the average flow and the turbulent energy (defined as the average of the kinetic energy of the fluctuations) arises
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\overline{K} = K_{\overline{\mathbf{u}}} + k \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Kinetic energy, \(K\).} Taking the dot\sphinxhyphen{}product of the NS equations with the velocity field, \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \text{NS}\), and exploiting product rule for derivatives,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\partial_t \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}}{2} + ( \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla ) \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}}{2} - \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \cdot \mathbb{S} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla P = 0\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As shown in the box below, the last two contributions can be rearranged to get
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{D K}{Dt} = \nabla \cdot \left( \nu \nabla K - P \mathbf{u} \right) - \nu | \nabla \mathbf{u} |^2 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Rearranging terms}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Assuming uniform viscosity \(\nu\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \cdot \mathbb{S} 
  & = \nu \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \cdot \left( \nabla \mathbf{u} + \nabla^T \mathbf{u} \right) = \\
  & = \nu \mathbf{u} \cdot \Delta \mathbf{u} = \\
  & = \nu \nabla \cdot \left( \left( \nabla \mathbf{u} \right) \cdot \mathbf{u} \right) - \nu \nabla \mathbf{u} : \nabla \mathbf{u} = \\
  & = \nabla \cdot \left(  \nu \nabla \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}}{2} \right) - \nu |\nabla \mathbf{u}|^2 \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
as \(\nabla \cdot \nabla^T \mathbf{u} = \partial_i \partial_j u_i = \partial_j u_{i/i} = 0\).

\sphinxAtStartPar

\begin{split}\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla P = \nabla \cdot ( P \mathbf{u} ) - P \underbrace{ \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} }_{=0} = \nabla \cdot ( P \mathbf{u} ) \ .\end{split}

\subsection{Dimensional analysis and the assumption of turbulence in equilibrium}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/rans_energy:dimensional-analysis-and-the-assumption-of-turbulence-in-equilibrium}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/rans_energy:fluid-mechanics-turbulence-rans-energy-turbulence-in-equilibrium}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A dimensional analysis of the equations of the kinetic energy of the average flow and turbulent energy helps in stating the concept of \sphinxstyleemphasis{turbulence in equilibrium} and its consequences.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Kinetic energy of the average field.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \frac{U^2}{T} \dfrac{\overline{D} K_{\overline{\mathbf{u}}}}{\overline{D}t} 
  = \frac{1}{L} \nabla \cdot \left( \frac{\nu U^2}{L} \nabla K_{\overline{\mathbf{u}}} - \mathscr{P} L \, \overline{\mathbf{u}' \otimes \mathbf{u}'} \cdot \overline{\mathbf{u}} - P U \overline{P} \overline{\mathbf{u}} \right) 
  + \mathscr{P} \nabla \overline{\mathbf{u}} : \overline{\mathbf{u}' \otimes \mathbf{u}'} - \frac{\nu U^2}{L^2} \nabla \overline{\mathbf{u}} : \nabla \overline{\mathbf{u}}
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Without an independent time scale, \(T = \frac{L}{U}\), and in incompressible flows \(P = U^2\)%
\begin{footnote}[3]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
Remember that, with some notational abuse, in this section \(P = \frac{P}{\rho}\).
%
\end{footnote}, and dividing for \(\frac{U^3}{L}\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \dfrac{\overline{D} K_{\overline{\mathbf{u}}}}{\overline{D}t}
  = - \nabla \cdot \left( \overline{P} \overline{\mathbf{u}} \right) + \frac{\nu}{U L} \left\{ \nabla \cdot \left( \nabla K_{\overline{\mathbf{u}}}  \right) - \nabla \overline{\mathbf{u}} : \nabla \overline{\mathbf{u}} \right\} - \frac{\mathscr{P} L}{U^3} \left\{ \nabla \cdot \left( \overline{\mathbf{u}' \otimes \mathbf{u}'} \cdot \overline{\mathbf{u}} \right) + \nabla \overline{\mathbf{u}} : \overline{\mathbf{u}' \otimes \mathbf{u}'} \right\}
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Turbulence is a phenomenon that occurs at high Reynolds numbers, i.e. with \(\frac{\nu}{U L} = \frac{1}{Re} \rightarrow 0\). If the other contributions have the same order of magnitude, it follows that \(\mathscr{P} = \frac{U^3}{L}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Turbulent energy.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\dfrac{u^2}{T} \dfrac{\overline{D} k}{\overline{D} t} = \frac{1}{L} \nabla \cdot \left( \frac{\nu u^2}{L} \nabla k - u^3 \overline{\mathbf{u}' k'} - p u \overline{ P' \mathbf{u}'}  \right) - \mathscr{P} \nabla \overline{\mathbf{u}} : \overline{\mathbf{u}' \otimes \mathbf{u}'} - \mathscr{D} \overline{\nabla \mathbf{u}' : \nabla \mathbf{u}'} \ ,
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\mathscr{D} = \frac{\nu U^2}{L^2}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Turbulence in equilibrium} means \(\mathscr{P} = \mathscr{D}\) and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathscr{P} = \mathscr{D} = \frac{U^3}{L} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\section{Scales of turbulence}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/kolmogorov:scales-of-turbulence}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/kolmogorov:fluid-mechanics-turbulence-rans-energy}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/kolmogorov::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Kolmogorov scales: large, inertial, viscous scales

\sphinxAtStartPar
Power\sphinxhyphen{}law for inertial scales…

\sphinxAtStartPar
Turbulence involves different characteristic scales%
\begin{footnote}[1]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
Roughly speaking, the characteristic dimension, velocity,… of the vortices. But what’s a vortex?
%
\end{footnote}, with their own characteristic length, time and relevant physical processes. While large scales usually depends on teh geometry of the flow, smaller scales have universal features for different flows: within this universal range, inertial subrange and dissipation range can be identified.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Large scales.}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Inertial subrange.} Assumption: turbulence in equilibrium. Spectral energy density \(E(\kappa)\)%
\begin{footnote}[2]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
Spectral energy density is defined as the energy density per unit wave\sphinxhyphen{}length, \(E = \int_{\kappa = 0}^{+\infty} E(\kappa) \, d \kappa\), and so it has physical dimension \([ E(\kappa) ] = [ E ][ L ] = L^3 T^{-2}\).
%
\end{footnote} is written as a function of dissipation \(\varepsilon\) (equal to production, in equilibrium), and a length scale \(\ell\) or a wave number \(\kappa\). From dimensional analysis
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[ E(\kappa) ] = \text{L}^3 \text{T}^{-2} \quad , \quad [ \varepsilon ] = \text{L}^2 \text{T}^{-3} \quad , \quad [ \kappa ] = \text{L}^{-1} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
it follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E \propto \varepsilon^{\frac{2}{3}} \kappa^{-\frac{5}{3}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Dimensional analysis}

\sphinxAtStartPar
From
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E = \varepsilon^\alpha \kappa^\beta \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
it follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
   3 = 2 \alpha - \beta \\
  -2 =-3 \alpha 
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus \(\alpha = \frac{2}{3}\) and \(\beta = \frac{4}{3} - 3 = - \frac{5}{3}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Kolmogorov scales.} Two relevant physical quantities: \(\nu\) kinematic viscosity, average rate of dissipation per unit\sphinxhyphen{}mass \(\varepsilon\) or \(\mathscr{D}\), with physical dimensions
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}[\nu] = \frac{\text{L}^2}{\text{T}} \quad , \quad [ \mathscr{D} ] = \frac{\text{L}^2}{\text{T}^3} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
With these two relevant physical quantities, it’s possible to build characteristic length, time, velocity and Reynolds number (built with the characteristic dimensions, no surprise it goes to 1)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\ell_{\eta} := \left( \frac{\nu^3}{\varepsilon} \right)^{\frac{1}{4}}  \quad , \quad 
\tau_{\eta} := \left( \frac{\nu}{\varepsilon} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}}  \quad , \quad 
   U_{\eta} := \frac{\ell_{\eta}}{\tau_{\eta}} = \left( \nu \varepsilon \right)^{\frac{1}{4}}  \quad , \quad 
  Re_{\eta} := \frac{U_{\eta} \ell_{\mu}}{\nu} = 1
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} evaluate the ratio of characteristic dimension of the viscous range with the chacteristic dimension of the problem in terms of Reynolds” number. Which assumptions to be made to get a Reynolds number of the large scales? Especially about \(\varepsilon\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Under the assumption of {\hyperref[\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/rans_energy:fluid-mechanics-turbulence-rans-energy-turbulence-in-equilibrium}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{turbulence in equilibrium}}}}, dimensional analysis gives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\varepsilon = \frac{U^3}{L} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\frac{\ell_{\eta}}{L} = \text{Re}^{-\frac{3}{4}} \quad , \quad
\frac{\tau_{\eta}}{T} = \text{Re}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \quad , \quad
\frac{U_{\eta}}{U} = \text{Re}^{-frac{1}{4}} \ .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These relation gives an estimate of the spatial resolution — i.e. the dimension of the mathematical problem — required by a numerical methods to fully resolve all the structures in the flow. In a 3\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional domain of side \(L\), grid spacing should be of order \(\Delta x \sim \ell_{\eta} \sim L \, \text{Re}^{-\frac{3}{4}}\), and thus the number of grid cells approximately \(N \sim \left\frac{L}{\ell_{\tau}}\right)^3 = \text{Re}^{\frac{9}{4}}\).


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxstepscope


\section{Boundary layer flows}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/boundary_layers:boundary-layer-flows}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/boundary_layers:fluid-mechanics-turbulence-boundary-layer-flows}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/boundary_layers::doc}}

\subsection{Prandtl equations}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/boundary_layers:prandtl-equations}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/boundary_layers:fluid-mechanics-turbulence-boundary-layer-flows-prandtl-eq}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Steady RANS equations for a 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional flow using Cartesian coordinates read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
  u \partial_x u + v \partial_y u + \partial_x \overline{u'u'} + \partial_y \overline{u'v'} - \nu \left( \partial_{xx} u + \partial_{yy} u \right) + \frac{1}{\rho} \partial_x P = 0 \\
  u \partial_x v + v \partial_y v + \partial_x \overline{u'v'} + \partial_y \overline{v'v'} - \nu \left( \partial_{xx} v + \partial_{yy} v \right) + \frac{1}{\rho} \partial_y P = 0 \\
  \partial_x u + \partial_y v = 0
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}


\sphinxAtStartPar
…
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
  u \partial_x u + v \partial_y u + \partial_y \left( \overline{u' v'} \right) - \nu \partial_{yy} u + \partial_x P = 0 \\
  \partial_y \overline{v'^2} + \partial_y P = 0 \\
  \partial_x u + \partial_y v = 0 \ ,
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As the Reynolds” number increases, the effect of the viscosity in the average flow may become negligible (for flows without solid surfaces, where viscous sublayer exists) if compared with the Reynolds” stress. In these situations, Prandtl equations become
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
  u \partial_x u + v \partial_y u + \partial_y \left( \overline{u' v'} \right) + \partial_x P = 0 \\
  \partial_y \overline{v'^2} + \partial_y P = 0 \\
  \partial_x u + \partial_y v = 0 \ ,
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Self\sphinxhyphen{}similar boundary layer flows}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/boundary_layers:self-similar-boundary-layer-flows}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/boundary_layers:fluid-mechanics-turbulence-boundary-layer-flows-self-similar}}

\subsubsection{Planar jet}
\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/boundary_layers:planar-jet}}\label{\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/10_turbolenza/boundary_layers:fluid-mechanics-turbulence-boundary-layer-flows-self-similar-planar-jet}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
From the \(y\)\sphinxhyphen{}component of the momentum, \(P + \overline{v'^2} = P_0(x)\), and 1) if the fluctuation becomes negligible in the outer flow and 2) the outer flow is irrotational with unifrom velocity, then pressure is uniform in the whole domain, \(P_0(x) = P_0\), and Prandtl equations from turbulent flows become
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
  u \partial_x u + v \partial_y u + \partial_y \left( \overline{u' v'} \right) = 0 \\
  \partial_x u + \partial_y v = 0 \ ,
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Self\sphinxhyphen{}similar solution.} Looking for a self\sphinxhyphen{}similar solution
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  u(x,y) & = U(x) f(\eta(x,y)) \\
  \overline{u'v'}(x,y) & = U^2(x) g(\eta(x,y)) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\eta(x,y) = \frac{y}{\delta(x)}\). Through the incompressibility constraint, the \(y\)\sphinxhyphen{}component of the velocity reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  v(x,y) - \underbrace{v(x,0)}_{=0}
  & = \int_{t = 0}^{y} \partial_y v(x,t) \, dt = \\
  & = - \int_{t=0}^{y} \partial_x u(x,t) \, dt = \\
  & = \int_{t=0}^{y} \left\{ -U'(x) f(\eta(x,t)) + U(x) \dfrac{df}{d \eta}(\eta(x,t)) \frac{t \delta'(x)}{\delta^2(x)} \right\} \, dt = \\
  & = \int_{\chi=0}^{\eta} \left\{ -U'(x) f(\eta(x,\delta(x) \chi)) \delta(x) + U(x) \dfrac{d f}{d \eta}(\eta(x, \delta(x) \chi)) \chi \delta'(x) \right\} \, d \chi \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\partial_x u(x,y) = U'(x) f(\eta(x,y)) - U(x) f'(\eta(x,y)) \frac{y \delta'(x)}{\delta^2(x)} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and having transformed the variable \(\chi = \frac{t}{\delta}\), and the extremes of integration accordingly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Mass, momentum and energy fluxes across normal planes.} Momentum flux reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}Q(x) = \int_{y=0}^{+\infty} u^2(x,y) \, dy \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Its derivative w.r.t. \(x\) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \dfrac{d}{dx} Q(x)
  & = \dfrac{d}{dx} \int_{y=-\infty}^{+\infty} u^2(x,y) \, dy = \\
  & = \int_{y=-\infty}^{+\infty} \partial_x u^2 \, dy = \\
  & = - \int_{y=-\infty}^{+\infty} \partial_y \left\{ uv + \overline{u'v'}  \right\} \, dy = 0 \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
if the flow is at rest at infinity. Using the self\sphinxhyphen{}similar assumption, this derivative reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \dfrac{d Q}{dx} = \dfrac{d}{dx} \left[ U^2(x) \delta(x) \int_{\eta=-\infty}^{+\infty} f^2(\eta) \, d \eta \right] \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that it follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \dfrac{d}{dx} \left( U^2(x) \delta(x) \right) = 2 U U' \delta + U^2 \delta' \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U' = - \dfrac{\delta'}{2\delta} U \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Mass flux.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}M(x) = \int_{y=-\infty}^{+\infty} u(x,y) \, dy \ , \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and, if the self\sphinxhyphen{}similarity assumption holds, its derivative reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\dfrac{d }{dx}M(x) = \dfrac{d}{dx} \left( U(x) \delta(x) \right) \int_{\eta=-\infty}^{+\infty} f(\eta) \, d\eta \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Energy flux.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}E(x) = \int_{y=-\infty}^{+\infty} \dfrac{1}{2} u^3(x,y) \, dy \ , \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and, if the self\sphinxhyphen{}similarity assumption holds, its derivative reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\dfrac{d }{dx}E(x) = \dfrac{d}{dx} \left( \dfrac{1}{2} U^3(x) \delta(x) \right) \int_{\eta=-\infty}^{+\infty} f(\eta) \, d\eta \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Solving for the self\sphinxhyphen{}similar solution.} Inserting the expressions of the velocity components and the turbulent stress into the \(x\)\sphinxhyphen{}component of the momentum equation,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0
  & = ( U f ) \left( U' f - U f' \eta \frac{\delta'}{\delta} \right) + \int_{\chi = 0}^{\eta} \left\{ -U' f \delta + U f' \chi \delta'  \right\} \, d\chi \, U f' \frac{1}{\delta} + U^2 g' \frac{1}{\delta} = \\
  & = U U' f^2 - U^2 f f' \eta \frac{\delta'}{\delta} - U U' f' \int_{\chi=0}^{\eta} f d \chi + U^2 f' \frac{\delta'}{\delta} \left(\left. \chi f \right|_{0}^{\eta} - \int_{\chi=0}^{\eta} f \, d \chi  \right)+ U^2 g' \frac{1}{\delta} = \\
  & = U U' f^2 - U U' f' \int_{\chi=0}^{\eta} f d \chi - U^2 f' \frac{\delta'}{\delta} \int_{\chi=0}^{\eta} f \, d \chi + U^2 g' \frac{1}{\delta}\ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and introducing the relation between the derivative of \(U(x)\) and \(\delta(x)\), and dividing by \(\frac{U^2}{\delta}\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{\delta'(x)}{2} \left[ f^2(\eta) + f'(\eta) \int_{\chi=0}^{\eta} f(\chi) d \chi \right] = g'(\eta) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For the existence of a self\sphinxhyphen{}similar solution, no coefficient can explicitly depend on \(x\) or \(y\), so the derivative of the boundary layer thickness must be constant
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\delta'(x) = S \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus a linear spreading is found,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\delta(x) - \delta(x_0) = S ( x - x_0 ) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As the momentum flux is constant in \(x\), it follows that — setting the origin of the coordinates so that \(\delta(x) = S x\) — the maximum velocity (velocity on the symmetry line of the jet) decreases as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}U(x) \propto \delta(x)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \propto x^{-\frac{1}{2}} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Mass flux goes with \(M(x) \sim x^{\frac{1}{2}}\) (increases, \sphinxstylestrong{entrainment}), while the energy flux goes with \(E(x) \sim x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\) (decreases due to dissipation).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Solution with constant turbulent viscosity as closure model.} With the assumption
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}- \overline{u'v'} = \nu_T \partial_y u \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
using self\sphinxhyphen{}similarity ansatz
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}-U^2 g = \nu_T U f' \frac{1}{\delta} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and with the additional assumption (\sphinxstylestrong{non\sphinxhyphen{}physical}, just to get a problem that can be solved analytically. An assumption more, an assumption less…),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{\nu}_T := \frac{\nu_T}{\delta(x) U(x)} = \text{const.} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the two non\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional functions \(f(\eta)\) and \(g(\eta)\) are related as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}g(\eta) = - \hat{\nu}_T f'(\eta) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus, the solution of the equation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{S}{2} \left[ f^2(\eta) + f'(\eta) \int_{\chi=0}^{\eta} f(\chi) d \chi  \right] + \hat{nu}_T f''(\eta) = 0 \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with the proper boundary conditions provides the non\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional velocity profile. Introducing the function \(F(\eta) = \int_{\chi=0}^{\eta} f(\chi) d \chi\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 0
 & = \frac{S}{2} \left( F'^{2}(\eta) + F''(\eta) F(\eta) \right) + \hat{\nu}T  F'''(\eta) = \\
 & = \frac{S}{2} \left( F(\eta) F'(\eta) \right)' + \hat{\nu}_T  F'''(\eta) \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Integrating once, and exploiting the boundary conditions (\sphinxstylestrong{todo}…)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0 
  & = \frac{S}{2} F(\eta) F'(\eta) + \hat{\nu}_T F''(\eta) =  \\
  & = \frac{S}{4} \left( F^2(\eta) \right)' + \hat{\nu}_T F''(\eta) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and integrating once again with the boundary condition \(F'(0) = 1\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{S}{4} F^2(\eta) = \hat{\nu}_T \left( 1 - F'(\eta) \right) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F'(\eta) = 1 - \frac{S}{4 \hat{\nu}_T} F^2(\eta) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Integrating one last time,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}F(\eta) = \frac{1}{\alpha} \text{tanh} \left( \alpha \eta \right) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\alpha = \sqrt{\frac{S}{4 \hat{\nu}_T}}\).

\part{Compressible Fluid Mechanics}

\sphinxstepscope


\chapter{Introduction to Compressible Fluid Mechanics}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/intro:introduction-to-compressible-fluid-mechanics}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/intro:compressible-intro}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/intro::doc}}\subsubsection*{Governing Equations}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
From compressible {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/governing-equations:compressible-governing-equations-navier-stokes}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxstylestrong{Navier\sphinxhyphen{}Stokes equations}}}}}, to {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/governing-equations:compressible-governing-equations-euler}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxstylestrong{Euler equations}}}}} for compressible fluids with negligible viscosity and heat conduction effects. Under these assumptions, the diffusive parts of the equations disappear, and discontinuities (e.g. {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/shock-normal:compressible-shocks-normal}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{normal shocks}}}}, {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/shock-oblique:compressible-shocks-oblique}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{oblique shocks}}}}, or \DUrole{xref,myst}{contact discontinuities}) may appear in the field: as fields are not differentiable and not even continuous across a discontinuity, differential equations fail and {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/jump-conditions:compressible-jump-conditions}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{jump conditions}}}} from integral equations are required to connect 2 regions of smooth fields.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The definition of {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/governing-equations:compressible-governing-equations-ideal}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxstylestrong{ideal flow}}}}} requires the additional assumption of absence of shocks, beside negligible viscosity and heat conduction. Without shocks, differential equations hold in the whole domain and {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/entropy:compressible-entropy}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{entropy equation}}}} shows that the flow is homoentropic, \(s(\mathbf{r},t) = \overline{s}\), if the inflow is uniform.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the flow is also irrotational, the governing equations can be written as a PDE for {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/potential-equation:compressible-irrotational-potential-equation}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{kinetic potential}}}}. Without shocks, differential equations hold in the whole domain and {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/vorticity:compressible-vorticity}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vorticity equation}}}} shows that the flow is irrotational in the whole domain if the inflow is irrotational.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/acoustics:compressible-acoustics}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Acoustics}}}} …linearized equations…

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Integral and differential form of the governing equations are provided, along with {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/jump-conditions:compressible-jump-conditions}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxstylestrong{jump conditions}}}}}: jump conditions play a crucial role in compressible inviscid flows governed by Euler equations where discontinuities (shocks and contact discontinuities) appear as a result of vanishing diffusion terms, in the limit of negligible viscous stress and heat conduction.
\subsubsection*{Vorticity, entropy and Bernoulli theorems}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Vorticity equation and entropy equation are discussed in detail in order to use them and their conclusions in different models of a flow.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/vorticity:compressible-vorticity}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Vorticity equation}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/entropy:compressible-entropy}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Entropy equation}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/bernoulli:compressible-bernoulli}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Bernoulli equation}}}}

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{Mathematical nature of equations of physics}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The (local) mathematical nature of the problem depends on the (local) value of the Mach number. As an example, for Euler equations%
\begin{footnote}[1]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
Dissipative terms make Navier\sphinxhyphen{}Stokes equations elliptic in steady conditions and parabolic in unsteady conditions.
%
\end{footnote} and derived models
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
in subsonic regions:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
in steady condition, the governing equations are elliptic

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
in unsteady condition, the governing equations are hyperbolic

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
in supersonic regions:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
in steady contditions, the governing equations are hyperbolic

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
in unsteady conditions, the governing equations are hyperbolic

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
As an example, the mathematical nature of governing equations of steady flows naturally apperas as a function of the (local) Mach number \(M\):
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
in the potential equation for irrotational homo\sphinxhyphen{}entropic flows. The (global) nature of the {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/potential-equation:compressible-irrotational-potential-equation-homoentropic-linearized-steady}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{linearized potential equation}}}} depends on the Mach number of the reference flow \(M_{\infty}\);

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
in the characteristic method for steady compressible flows (\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{collect all the material, now here and there, e.g. in Math:PDE:hyperbolic equations}): in a d\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional domain, \(d+2\) families of characteristic surfaces exist in supersonic regions, while only \(d\) families exist in subsonic flows. Thus, it’s not possible to use the method of characteristics: the solution in a point \(P\) is not function of the values of \(d+2\) variables on the \(d+2\) characteristic lines through \(P\), but depends on the solution in its neighborhood (typical condition for elliptic equations).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Introduction to hyperbolic problems:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Link to Math jbook: hyperbolic problems, method of characteristics, integral balance, jumps,…

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
include script avaiable on GDrive in \(\texttt{fvm}\) folder

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{Canonical flows}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
1\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional ideal flow

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/quasi-1d:compressible-quasi-1d}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{quasi 1\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional flows}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/quasi-1d-non-ideal:compressible-quasi-1d-non-ideal}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{(quasi) 1\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional non\sphinxhyphen{}ideal flows}}}}: with friction (Fanno), and with heat flux (Rayleigh)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional flows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
shocks: {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/shock-normal:compressible-shocks-normal}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{normal shocks}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/shock-oblique:compressible-shocks-oblique}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{oblique shocks}}}} (\(\theta - \beta - M \))

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
rarefaction waves: {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/prandtl-meyer:compressible-prandtl-meyer}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Prandtl\sphinxhyphen{}Meyer exapnsion}}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
discontituities

\end{itemize}

\chapter{Governing equations}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/governing-equations:governing-equations}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/governing-equations:compressible-governing-equations}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/governing-equations::doc}}

\section{Compressible Navier\sphinxhyphen{}Stokes equations}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/governing-equations:compressible-navier-stokes-equations}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/governing-equations:compressible-governing-equations-navier-stokes}}\subsubsection*{Integral balance equations}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Integral balance equations of mass (Lavoisier principle), momentum (Second principle of Newton dynamics) and total energy (Principle of energy conservation) for a control volume \(V\) at rest read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \dfrac{d}{dt} \int_V \rho + \oint_{\partial V} \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = 0 \\
  & \dfrac{d}{dt} \int_V \rho \mathbf{u} + \oint_{\partial V} \rho \mathbf{u} \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \int_{V} \rho \mathbf{g} + \oint_{\partial V} \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} \\
  & \dfrac{d}{dt} \int_V \rho e^t + \oint_{\partial V} \rho e^t \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \int_{V} \rho \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{u} + \oint_{\partial V} \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{u} - \oint_{\partial V} \mathbf{q} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Differential balance equations}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Differential balance equations in conservative form follow from regularity of the functions involved in the equations and from the arbitrariness of the control volume \(V\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \partial_t \rho + \nabla \cdot ( \rho \mathbf{u} ) = 0 \\
  & \partial_t \left( \rho \mathbf{u} \right) + \nabla \cdot ( \rho \mathbf{u} \otimes \mathbf{u} ) = \rho \mathbf{g} + \nabla \cdot \mathbb{T} \\
  & \partial_t \left( \rho e^t        \right) + \nabla \cdot ( \rho \mathbf{u} e^t ) = \rho \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{u} + \nabla \cdot ( \mathbb{T} \cdot \mathbf{u} ) - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\mathbb{T}\) the stress tensor, relating stress vector \(\mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}}\) on the a surface and unit normal \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) of that surface via \sphinxstylestrong{Cauchy relation}, \(\mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} = \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbb{T}\),

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(e^t\) the total energy, \(e^t = e + \frac{|\mathbf{u}|^2}{2}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\mathbf{q}\) heat flux by conduction.

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{Constitutive equations and equations of state}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The problem is completed with initial and boundary conditions, along with constitutive equations and equations of state. As an example:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A \sphinxstylestrong{Newtonian fluid} is defined by the constitutive equation for stress
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbb{T} = - p \mathbb{I} + \mathbb{S} = - p \mathbb{I} + 2 \mu \mathbb{D} + \lambda ( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} ) \mathbb{I} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(p\) the pressure field, \(\mu\), \(\lambda\) viscosity coefficients, and \(\mathbb{D}\) the deformation velocity tensor. In general, they are function of the thermodynamic state.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Fourier law} for heat flux by conduction for an isotropic medium reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{q} = - k \nabla T \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Equations of state} relate non\sphinxhyphen{}dynamical physical variables to the dynamical variables, to get a well\sphinxhyphen{}defined problem from the mathematical point of view with the same numeber of equations and unknowns. A pair of independent thermodynamic variables are required to define a thermodynamic state. As an example, using \((\rho, e)\) as the pair of independent thermodynamic variables (fields here, with the local equilibrium assumption), equations of state need to provide the expression of pressure and temperature (and viscosity and conduction coefficients, if they can’t be treated as constant parameters),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
     p(\rho, e) \ , \quad T(\rho, e) \ ,  \quad \dots
   \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{itemize}


\section{Euler equations}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/governing-equations:euler-equations}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/governing-equations:compressible-governing-equations-euler}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Neglecting viscosity and heat conduction, diffusive contributions (usually containing second\sphinxhyphen{}order spatial derivatives of the unknowns) drop and Navier\sphinxhyphen{}Stokes equations become Euler equations. Where differential equations hold (in absence of shoscks and discontinuities), local governing equations read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \partial_t \rho + \nabla \cdot ( \rho \mathbf{u} ) = 0 \\
  & \partial_t \left( \rho \mathbf{u} \right) + \nabla \cdot ( \rho \mathbf{u} \otimes \mathbf{u} + p \mathbb{I} ) = \rho \mathbf{g} \\
  & \partial_t \left( \rho e^t        \right) + \nabla \cdot \left( \rho \mathbf{u}  \left( e^t + \frac{p}{\rho} \right) \right) = \rho \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{u} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Constitutive equations.} There’s no need to constitutive equations for viscous stress and heat flux by conduction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Equations of state.} Two thermodynamic variables (fields) have dynamical equations (in the conservative form, density and total energy \((\rho, e^t)\)), while \sphinxstylestrong{only one} other thermodynamic variable doesn’t have a dynamical equation, here pressure field \(p\). Thus, \sphinxstylestrong{only one equation of state} is required to write a well\sphinxhyphen{}defined mathematical problem
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p(\rho, e) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
while other dependent theromdynamic variables (fields), like temperature \(T\), can be retrieved a posteriori once the problem is solved.


\section{Ideal flow}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/governing-equations:compressible-governing-equations-ideal}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/governing-equations:ideal-flow}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The definition of an ideal flow immediately follows from the {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/entropy:compressible-entropy}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{entropy equation}}}}: in a fluid with negligible viscosity and heat conduction, where no shock occurs (and thus where differential equations hold in the whole domain), the entropy of each material particle is constant.


\section{Other form of the governing equations}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/governing-equations:other-form-of-the-governing-equations}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/governing-equations:compressible-governing-equations-other}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/potential-equation:compressible-irrotational-potential-equation}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxstylestrong{Potential equation for irrotational compressible flows}}}}}. Some flow of interest \sphinxhyphen{} e.g. in aeronautics \sphinxhyphen{} are irrotational flow. It can be proved with {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/vorticity:compressible-vorticity}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vorticity equation}}}} that an irrotational inflow produces irrotational flow in the whole domain, if viscoisty effects are negligible and no oblique shock occurs.

\section{Perfect Ideal Gas (PIG)}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/pig:perfect-ideal-gas-pig}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/pig:compressible-pig}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/pig::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Add details, and link to \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-physics-thermodynamics/intro.html}{Thermodynamics} to deal with thermodynamic potentials, coefficients and derivatives in the most general way}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Equation of state.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p = \rho R T \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(R = \frac{R_u}{M_m}\), being \(M_m\) the molar mass of the gas and \(R_u\) the \sphinxstylestrong{universal gas constant}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R_u = 8134.46 \frac{\text{J}}{\text{kmol} \, \text{K}} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\label{ch/compressible/pig:example-0}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Example 13.1.1 (Molar mass of dry air \sphinxhyphen{} mixture of gas)}



\sphinxAtStartPar
Let the composition of dry air: \(\text{N}_2: \, 78.08\%\), \(\text{O}_2: \, 20.95 \%\), \(\text{Ar}: \, 0.93 \%\), \(\text{CO}_2: \, 0.04\%\)

\sphinxAtStartPar
…
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}M_{m, air} = 28.97 \, \frac{\text{kg}}{\text{kmol}} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus the value of gas constant for dry air is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R_{air} = \frac{R_u}{M_{m,air}} = \frac{8314.46 \frac{\text{J}}{\text{kmol} \,\text{K}}}{ 28.97 \frac{\text{kg}}{\text{kmol}}} = 287.00 \frac{\text{J}}{\text{kg} \, \text{K}} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Internal energy and enthalpy.} In perfect ideal gas, energy and enthalpy are function of temperature only, with constant heat coefficients \(c_v\), \(c_p\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  e & = c_v T \\
  h & = c_p T 
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Heat coefficient ratio.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\gamma = \frac{c_p}{c_v}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Meyer relation.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}c_p - c_v = R\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \frac{c_v}{R} & = \frac{     1}{\gamma-1} \\
  \frac{c_p}{R} & = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1} 
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Entropy.} Starting from the first principle of thermodynamics
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}de = T ds + \frac{p}{\rho^2} d \rho \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(d e = c_v dT\), it’s possible to write the differential of entropy as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  d s
  & = c_v \frac{dT}{T} - R \frac{d \rho}{\rho} = \\
  & = c_v \frac{dp}{p} - c_p \frac{d \rho}{\rho} = \\
  & = c_p \frac{dT}{T} - R \frac{d p}{p} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
having used the equation of state, Meyer relation and the relation between differentials of thermodynamic quantities, like
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{d T}{T} = \frac{ d\left(\frac{p}{\rho R} \right)}{ \frac{p}{\rho R} } = \frac{\rho}{p} \left( \frac{dp}{\rho} - \frac{p}{\rho^2} d \rho \right) = \frac{dp}{p} - \frac{d \rho}{\rho} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The finite difference between two thermodynamic states immediately follows from integration (being \(R\), \(c_v\), \(c_p\) constant for a PIG),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  s - s_0
  & = c_v \ln \left( \frac{T}{T_0} \right) - R   \ln \left( \frac{\rho}{\rho_0} \right) = \\
  & = c_v \ln \left( \frac{p}{p_0} \right) - c_p \ln \left( \frac{\rho}{\rho_0} \right) = \\
  & = c_p \ln \left( \frac{T}{T_0} \right) - R   \ln \left( \frac{   p}{   p_0} \right) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Speed of sound.} The speed of sound in a medium is defined as%
\begin{footnote}[1]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
The definition of the speed of sound naturally appears in \DUrole{xref,myst}{acoustics} and in the method of characteristic for hyperbolic problems, like unsteady Euler equations…
%
\end{footnote}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}a^2 = \left( \dfrac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_s \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For a PIG, relation (\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Add ref}) links pressure, density and entropy. This relation can be recast as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{p}{p_0}(\rho, s; \rho_0, s_0) = \frac{\rho^\gamma}{\rho_0^\gamma} e^{ (\gamma-1) \frac{s-s_0}{R} } \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Direct evaluation of the partial derivative at constant \(s\) gives the expression of speed of sound for a PIG
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}a^2 = \gamma R T = \gamma \frac{p}{\rho} \end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Details}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  a^2
  & = \left( \dfrac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_s = \\
  & = \left( \dfrac{\partial}{\partial \rho} \right)_s \frac{\rho^{\gamma}}{\rho_0^{\gamma}} e^{(\gamma-1)\frac{s-s_0}{R}} = \\
  & = \gamma \rho^{-1} \frac{\rho^{\gamma}}{\rho_0^{\gamma}} e^{(\gamma-1)\frac{s-s_0}{R}} = \\
  & = \gamma \frac{p}{\rho} = \\
  & = \gamma R T \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\bigskip\hrule\bigskip

\section{Real Gas \sphinxhyphen{} Van der Waals}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/vdw:real-gas-van-der-waals}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/vdw:compressible-vdw}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/vdw::doc}}

\chapter{Jump conditions}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/jump-conditions:jump-conditions}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/jump-conditions:compressible-jump-conditions}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/jump-conditions::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Continuous medium.} Jump conditions for a continuous medium read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0          & = [ \rho u^{rel}_n ]  \\
  \mathbf{0} & = \dot{m}[ \mathbf{u} ] - [ \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} ] \\
  0          & = \dot{m}[ e^t ] + [ \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{u} - \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{q} ]  \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(\dot{m} = \rho_1 u^{rel}_{n,1} = \rho_2 u^{rel}_{n,2}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Inviscid flows, w/o heat conduction (Euler equations).} If viscous stress and heat conduction are negligible (as they’re in Euler equations), jump conditions become
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0          & = [ \rho u^{rel}_n ]  \\
  \mathbf{0} & = \dot{m}[ \mathbf{u} ] + [ p \mathbf{n} ] \\
  0          & = \dot{m}[ h^t ] + [ p ] \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{u}_s  \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Details}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Starting from integral equations
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \dfrac{d}{dt} \int_{v_t} \rho + \oint_{\partial v_t} \rho \mathbf{u}^{rel} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = 0 \\
  & \dfrac{d}{dt} \int_{v_t} \rho \mathbf{u} + \oint_{\partial v_t} \rho \mathbf{u} \mathbf{u}^{rel} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \int_{v_t} \rho \mathbf{g}  + \oint_{\partial v_t} \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} \\
  & \dfrac{d}{dt} \int_{v_t} \rho e^t + \oint_{\partial v_t} \rho e^t \mathbf{u}^{rel} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \int_{v_t} \rho \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{u}  + \oint_{\partial v_t} \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{u} - \oint_{\partial v_t} \mathbf{q} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and collapsing the volume \(v_t\) on one of its dimension, volume contributions become negligible when compared to surface contributions. Jump conditions immeadiately follow, setting \(\hat{\mathbf{n}} = \hat{\mathbf{n}}_2 = - \hat{\mathbf{n}}_1\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0          & = [ \rho u^{rel}_n ]  \\
  \mathbf{0} & = [ \rho \mathbf{u} u^{rel}_n - \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} ] \\
  0          & = [ \rho e^t u^{rel}_n + \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{u} - \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{q} ]  \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus \(\rho_1 u_{n,1}^{rel} = \rho_2 u_{n,2}^{rel} = \dot{m}\), and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0          & = [ \rho u^{rel}_n ]  \\
  \mathbf{0} & = \dot{m}[ \mathbf{u} ] - [ \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} ] \\
  0          & = \dot{m}[ e^t ] + [ \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{u} - \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{q} ]  \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If viscous streass and conduction heat flux are negligible,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0          & = [ \rho u^{rel}_n ]  \\
  \mathbf{0} & = \dot{m}[ \mathbf{u} ] + [ p \mathbf{n} ] \\
  0          & = \dot{m}[ e^t ] + [ p \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{u} ] = \\
             & = \dot{m}[ e^t ] + \left[ \frac{p}{\rho} \underbrace{\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \rho ( \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_s )}_{ \rho u_{n}^{rel} = \dot{m}} + p \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{u}_s \right] = \\
             & = \dot{m} \left[ e^t + \frac{p}{\rho} \right] + [ p \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{u}_s ] = \\
             & = \dot{m} \left[ h^t \right] + \left[ p \right] \, \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{u}_s  \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Two main cases are determined by the value of the mass flow \(\dot{m}\):
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
if \(\dot{m} = 0\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
     & \dot{m} = 0 \\
     & [ p ] = 0 \ ,
   \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
while nothing can be said about the tangential component of the velocity field and the total enthalpy. These conditions hold \sphinxstylestrong{contact discontinuities}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
if \(\dot{m} \ne 0\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
     0 & = [ \dot{m} ] = [ \rho u_{n}^{rel} ]   \\
     \mathbf{0} & = \dot{m} [ \mathbf{u}_{\mathbf{t}} ]  \\
     0 & = \dot{m} [ u_n ] + [ \, p \, ] = \dot{m} [ u_n^{rel} ] + [ \, p \, ]  \\
     0 & = \dot{m} [ h^{t,rel} ] = \dot{m} [ h^{t,rel}_n ] 
   \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These conditions hold for \sphinxstylestrong{shocks} (usually compression shocks, e.g. for PIG, but for heavy fluids expansion shocks may exist as well).

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{Details}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0 & = [ \dot{m} ] = [ \rho u_{n}^{rel} ]   \\
  \mathbf{0} & = \dot{m} [ \mathbf{u}_{\mathbf{t}} ]  \\
  0 & = \dot{m} [ u_n ] + [ \, p \, ] =  && ([u_s] = 0) \\
    & = \dot{m} [ u_n - u_s ] + [ \, p \, ] = \\
    & = \dot{m} [ u_n^{rel} ] + [ \, p \, ]  \\
  0 & = \dot{m} [ h^t ] + u_{s,n} [ \, p \, ] = \\
    & = \dot{m} \left[ h^t \right] - u_{s,n} \, \dot{m} \left[ u_n \right] = \\
    & = \dot{m} \left[ h + \frac{u_n^2 + u_t^2}{2} - u_{s,n} u_n  \right] = \\
    & = \dot{m} \left[ h + \frac{u_n^2 - 2 u_{s,n} u_n + u_{s,n}^2}{2} - \frac{u_{s,n}^2}{2} + \frac{u_t^2}{2}  \right] = \\
    & = \dot{m} \left[ h + \frac{(u_n - u_{s,n})^2}{2} - \frac{u_{s,n}^2}{2} + \frac{u_t^2}{2}  \right] = \\
    & = \dot{m} \left[ h^{t,rel} \right] = \\
    & = \dot{m} \left[ h^{t,rel}_n \right] \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
as \(\left[ u_{s,n}^2 \right] = 0\) being \(u_{s,n}\) the velocity of the «discontinuity» surface, \([ \mathbf{u}_t ] = 0\) from the tangential component of the momentum equation, and with the definition of the \sphinxstyleemphasis{relative total enthalpy}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}h^{t,rel} := h + \frac{1}{2} \left( (u_n - u_{s,n})^2 + u_t^2  \right) = h + \frac{1}{2} \left( \left( u_{n}^{rel} \right)^2 + u_t^2 \right) \ , \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and \(h^{t,rel}_n\) the relative total enthalpy built with the normal component of the relative velocity only.

\sphinxstepscope


\chapter{Bernoulli’s theorem in compressible fluid mechanics}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/bernoulli:bernoulli-s-theorem-in-compressible-fluid-mechanics}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/bernoulli:compressible-bernoulli}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/bernoulli::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Assuming no discontinuity occurs in physical quantities (reasonable for viscous and diffusive fluids?), the differential form of governing equations holds.
Starting from governing equations of compressible fluids,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \dfrac{D \rho}{D t} = - \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} \\
  & \rho \dfrac{D \mathbf{u}}{D t} = \rho \mathbf{g} + \nabla \cdot \mathbb{T} \\
  & \rho \dfrac{D e^t}{D t} = \rho \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{u} + \nabla \cdot (\mathbb{T} \cdot \mathbf{u}) - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with the stress tensor sum of a pressure and viscous contribution, \(\mathbb{T} = - p \mathbb{I} + \mathbb{S}\). For Newtonian fluids, viscous stress tensor can be written as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbb{S} = 2 \mu \mathbb{D} + \lambda \left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} \right) \mathbb{I} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Total energy per unit mass \(e^t\) is the sum of internal and kinetic energy, \(e^t = e + \frac{|\mathbf{u}|^2}{2}\). Total derivative operator reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\dfrac{D}{Dt} = \dfrac{\partial }{\partial t} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Total energy equation can be recast as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \left[ \nabla e^t - \mathbf{g} - \frac{1}{\rho} \nabla \cdot \mathbb{T} \right] = - \rho \dfrac{\partial e^t}{\partial t} + \nabla \mathbf{u} : \mathbb{T} - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q} \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Keeping only conservative (pressure) contributions to stress on the LHS
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \left[ \nabla e^t - \mathbf{g} + \frac{1}{\rho} \nabla P \right] & = - \rho \dfrac{\partial e^t}{\partial t} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \cdot \mathbb{S} - P \, \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} + \nabla \mathbf{u} : \mathbb{S} - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q} \\
  \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \left[ \nabla  e^t + \nabla \chi + \frac{1}{\rho} \nabla P \right] & = - \rho \dfrac{\partial e^t}{\partial t} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \cdot \mathbb{S} + \dfrac{P}{\rho} \dfrac{D \rho}{D t} + \nabla \mathbf{u} : \mathbb{S} - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q} \\
  \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \left[ \nabla  e^t + \nabla \chi + \frac{1}{\rho} \nabla P \right] & = - \rho \dfrac{\partial e^t}{\partial t} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \cdot \mathbb{S} + \dfrac{P}{\rho} \dfrac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \dfrac{P}{\rho} \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \rho + \nabla \mathbf{u} : \mathbb{S} - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q} \\
  \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \left[ e^t + \chi + \frac{P}{\rho} \right] & = - \rho \dfrac{\partial e^t}{\partial t} + \dfrac{P}{\rho} \dfrac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbb{S} \cdot \mathbf{u} \right) - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q} \\
  \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \left[ e^t + \chi + \frac{P}{\rho} \right] & = - \rho \dfrac{\partial e^t}{\partial t} + \underbrace{\dfrac{P}{\rho} \dfrac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} - \rho \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial t}}_{= - \rho \frac{\partial }{\partial t} \left( \frac{P}{\rho} \right)} + \rho \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbb{S} \cdot \mathbf{u} \right) - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q} \\
  \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \left[ e^t + \chi + \frac{P}{\rho} \right] & = - \rho \dfrac{\partial }{\partial t} \left( e^t + \dfrac{P}{\rho} \right) + \rho \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbb{S} \cdot \mathbf{u} \right) - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\label{None:theorem-0}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Theorem  (Bernoulli’s theorem for compressible flow on streamlines)}



\sphinxAtStartPar
Now, for steady flows \(\frac{\partial }{\partial t} \equiv 0\), with negligible viscous stress \(\mathbb{S} \equiv \mathbb{0}\) and heat conduction \(\mathbf{q} \equiv 0\), \sphinxstylestrong{Bernoulli’s polynomial is constant for every point of a streamline}, as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \left[ e + \dfrac{|\mathbf{u}|^2}{2} + \frac{P}{\rho} + \chi \right] = 0 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\end{sphinxadmonition}
\label{None:theorem-1}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Theorem  (Dynamical equation for total enthalpy)}



\sphinxAtStartPar
Governing equations of fluid mechanics can be recast to get a dynamical equation for the total enthaply \(h^t = e^t + \frac{P}{\rho}\), whose convective form reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho \dfrac{D h^t}{D t} = - \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \chi + \rho \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbb{S} \cdot \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{q} \right) \ . \end{split}
\end{equation*}\end{sphinxadmonition}
\label{None:theorem-2}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Theorem  (Dynamical equation for Bernoulli’s polynomial)}



\sphinxAtStartPar
If the conservative force field per unit mass \(\mathbf{g} = - \nabla \chi\) has no explicit dependence on time, \(\partial_t \chi = 0\) and \(D_t \chi = \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \chi\), it’s possible to write a dynamical equation for the Bernoulli’s polynomial, \(B = h^t + \chi\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho \dfrac{D B}{D t} = \rho \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbb{S} \cdot \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{q} \right) \ , \end{split}
\end{equation*}\end{sphinxadmonition}

\chapter{Vorticity equation}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/vorticity:vorticity-equation}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/vorticity:compressible-vorticity}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/vorticity::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A differential equation governing vorticity can be derived starting from the momentum equation. Starting from the convective form of the momentum equation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \partial_t \mathbf{u} + \left( \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \right) \mathbf{u} 
  & = \mathbf{g} + \dfrac{1}{\rho} \nabla \cdot \left[ - p \mathbb{I} + 2 \mu \mathbb{D} + \lambda \left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} \right) \mathbb{I} \right] = \\
  & = \mathbf{g} - \dfrac{1}{\rho} \nabla p + \frac{1}{\rho} \left[ 2 \mu \nabla^2 \mathbf{u} + \left( \mu + \lambda \right) \nabla \left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} \right) \right] \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  2 \nabla \cdot \mathbb{D} & = \partial_i \left( \partial_i u_j + \partial_j u_i \right) = u_{j/ji} + u_{i/jj} = \nabla \left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} \right) + \nabla^2 \mathbf{u} \\
  \nabla \cdot \left( \left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} \right) \mathbb{I} \right) & = \partial_{k} \left( u_{l/l} \delta_{ki} \right) = u_{l/li} = \nabla \left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} \right) \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Taking the curl of the momentum equation above, vorticity equation follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
\partial_t \boldsymbol\omega + \nabla \times \left( \boldsymbol\omega \times \mathbf{u} \right) & = - \nabla \times \frac{\nabla p}{\rho} + \dots \\
\partial_t \boldsymbol\omega + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \boldsymbol\omega - \boldsymbol\omega \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u} + \boldsymbol\omega \, \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} & = \frac{1}{\rho^2}  \nabla \rho \times \nabla p + \dots  \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or, highlighting the material derivative,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
  D_t \boldsymbol\omega = \boldsymbol\omega \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u} - \boldsymbol\omega \, \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} + \frac{1}{\rho^2}  \nabla \rho \times \nabla p + \dots  \ .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Vector caluclus identities}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\nabla \left( \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} \right) = a_{i/j} b_i + a_i b_{i/j}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \left(\nabla \times \mathbf{a} \right) \times \mathbf{b} 
  & = \varepsilon_{ijk} \varepsilon_{jlm} \partial_l a_m b_k = \\
  & = \left( \delta_{kl} \delta_{im} - \delta_{km} \delta_{il} \right) \partial_l a_m b_k = \\
  & = a_{i/k} b_k - a_{k/i} b_k = \mathbf{b} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{a} - \nabla \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} 
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus, \(\left(\nabla \times \mathbf{u}\right) \times \mathbf{u}\) can be written as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left(\nabla \times \mathbf{u}\right) \times \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u} - \nabla \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u} =  \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u} - \nabla \frac{|\mathbf{u}|^2}{2} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that the advective term can be recast as \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u} = \boldsymbol\omega \times \mathbf{u} - \nabla \frac{|\mathbf{u}|^2}{2} \ ,\)

\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(\boldsymbol\omega = \nabla \times \mathbf{u}\) the vorticity field. Using vector calculus identity
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \nabla \times \left( \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} \right)  
  & = \varepsilon_{ijk} \partial_j \varepsilon_{klm} \left( a_l b_m \right) = \\
  & = \left( \delta_{il} \delta_{jm} - \delta_{im} \delta_{jl} \right) \partial_j \left( a_l b_m \right) = \\
  & = a_{i/j} b_j + a_i b_{j/j} - a_{j/j} b_i - a_j b_{i/j} = \\
  & = \mathbf{b} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{a} \, \nabla \cdot \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{b} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{a} - \mathbf{a} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{b} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and recalling that the curl of a gradient is identically zero, the curl of the advective term reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \nabla \times \left[ \left( \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \right) \mathbf{u} \right] 
  & = \nabla \times \left[ \boldsymbol\omega \times \mathbf{u} + \nabla \frac{|\mathbf{u}|^2}{2} \right] = \\
  & = \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \boldsymbol\omega + \boldsymbol\omega \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u} \underbrace{\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol\omega}_{ = \mathbf{0} \, \text{div  curl}\equiv\mathbf{0}} - \boldsymbol\omega \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The curl of a Laplacian reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left\{ \nabla \times \nabla^2 \mathbf{u} \right\}_i = \varepsilon_{ijk} \partial_j \partial_{ll} u_k = \partial_{ll} \left( \varepsilon_{ijk} \partial_j u_k \right) = \nabla^2 \left( \nabla \times \mathbf{u} \right) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The curl of the product of a scalar and vector field reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\nabla \times \left( a \mathbf{v} \right) = \varepsilon_{ijk} \partial_j ( a v_k ) =  \varepsilon_{ijk} \left( a_{/j} v_k + a v_{k/j} \right) = \nabla a \times \mathbf{v} + a \nabla \times \mathbf{v} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\chapter{Potential equation for irrotational compressible flows}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/potential-equation:potential-equation-for-irrotational-compressible-flows}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/potential-equation:compressible-irrotational-potential-equation}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/potential-equation::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Under the assumption of irrotational flow%
\begin{footnote}[1]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
Vorticity is confined in thin layers, like boundary layers and wakes, modelled as tangential velocity discontinuities.
%
\end{footnote}, the velocity field \(\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{r},t)\) can be written as a gradient of a scalar potential \(\phi(\mathbf{r},t)\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\nabla \times \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0} \quad \rightarrow \quad \mathbf{u} = \nabla \phi \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Euler equations in convective form with independent variables \((\rho, \mathbf{u}, s)\) read%
\begin{footnote}[2]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
\(\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u} = \nabla \frac{|\mathbf{u}|^2}{2} + \boldsymbol\omega \times \mathbf{u}\), with \(\boldsymbol = \nabla \times \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}\) in irrotational flows.
%
\end{footnote}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \partial_t \rho + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \rho + \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0 \\
  & \partial_t \mathbf{u} + \nabla \frac{|\mathbf{u}|^2}{2} + \frac{\nabla p}{\rho} = \mathbf{0} \\
  & \partial_t s + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla s = 0 \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\section{Homoentropic flows}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/potential-equation:homoentropic-flows}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/potential-equation:compressible-irrotational-potential-equation-homoentropic}}

If no shock occurs and the inflow is uniform, the flow is homoentropic, \(s(\mathbf{r},t) = \overline{s}\). Mass and momentum equations become
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}

  & \partial_t \nabla \phi + \nabla \frac{|\nabla \phi|^2}{2} + a^2(\rho, \overline{s}) \frac{\nabla \rho}{\rho} = \mathbf{0} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(a^2(\rho, \overline{s}) = \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_s\) the square of the speed of sound.

with the differential operator \sphinxhyphen{} here applied twice%
\begin{footnote}[3]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
\(D^{\mathbf{u}_\infty}_{tt} \varphi := D^{\mathbf{u}_\infty}_{t} \left( D^{\mathbf{u}_\infty}_{t} \varphi \right)\) \(= (\partial_t + \mathbf{u}_\infty \cdot \nabla) (\partial_t \varphi + \mathbf{u}_\infty \cdot \nabla \varphi)\) \(= \partial_{tt} \varphi + 2 \mathbf{u} \cdot \partial_t \nabla \varphi + \mathbf{u}_\infty \cdot \nabla ( \mathbf{u}_\infty \cdot \nabla \varphi)\).
%
\end{footnote} \sphinxhyphen{} \(D^{\mathbf{u}_\infty}_t = \partial_t + \mathbf{u}_\infty \cdot \nabla\) representing advection with the free\sphinxhyphen{}stream velocity field \(\mathbf{u}_\infty\).
\subsubsection*{Details}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0
  & = \partial_{tt} \phi - a^2 \nabla^2 \phi + \partial_t |\nabla \phi|^2 + \nabla \phi \cdot \nabla \frac{|\nabla \phi|^2}{2} = \\
  & = \partial_{tt} \varphi - ( a^2_\infty + {a'}^2 ) \nabla^2 \varphi + 2 \partial_t ( \nabla \phi \cdot \mathbf{u}_\infty + \dots ) + \mathbf{u}_\infty \cdot \nabla \left( \mathbf{u}_\infty \cdot \nabla \varphi + \dots \right) \simeq \\
  & = \partial_{tt} \varphi - a^2_{\infty} \nabla^2 \varphi + 2 \mathbf{u}_\infty \cdot \partial_t \nabla \phi + \mathbf{u}_\infty \cdot \nabla ( \mathbf{u}_\infty \cdot \nabla \varphi ) \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Introducing the \sphinxstyleemphasis{linear} differential operator
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}D^{\mathbf{u}_\infty}_t := \partial_t + \mathbf{u}_\infty \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
the linearized equation can be re\sphinxhyphen{}written as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}D^{\mathbf{u}_\infty}_{tt} \varphi - a^2_\infty \nabla^2 \varphi = 0 \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(D^{\mathbf{u}_\infty}_{tt}\) the operator applied twice, \(D^{\mathbf{u}_\infty}_{tt} = D^{\mathbf{u}_\infty}_{t}D^{\mathbf{u}_\infty}_{t}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Introducing a set of Cartesian coordinates with the \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\)\sphinxhyphen{}axis aligned with the free\sphinxhyphen{}stream velocity \(\mathbf{u}_\infty = U_{\infty} \hat{\mathbf{x}}\), the differential operator can be written as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}D_t^{\mathbf{u}_\infty} = \partial_t + U_\infty \partial_x \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and the linearized equation of the potential becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\varphi_{tt} + 2 U_\infty \partial_{xt} \varphi + U_\infty^2 \varphi_{xx} - a_\infty^2 \left( \varphi_{xx} + \varphi_{yy} + \varphi_{zz} \right) = 0 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Linearized steady potential equation \sphinxhyphen{} Prandtl\sphinxhyphen{}Glauert transformation}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/potential-equation:linearized-steady-potential-equation-prandtl-glauert-transformation}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/potential-equation:compressible-irrotational-potential-equation-homoentropic-linearized-steady}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Steady equation becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}(1-M_\infty^2) \varphi_{xx} + \varphi_{yy} + \varphi_{zz} = 0 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This equation can be transformed into a Laplace equation (the same equation governing the potential for incompressible flows) with a transformation of coordinates
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \widetilde{x} & = \frac{ x }{ \sqrt{1 - M_\infty^2} } \\
 \widetilde{y} & = y                       \\
 \widetilde{z} & = z                       \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{\partial \widetilde{x}}{\partial x} = \frac{1}{ \sqrt{1 - M^2} } \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\varphi_{\widetilde{x} \widetilde{x}} + \varphi_{\widetilde{y} \widetilde{y}} + \varphi_{\widetilde{z} \widetilde{z}} = 0 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Details}

\sphinxAtStartPar
With
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\widetilde{x} = \beta x \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
it follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{\partial}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial \widetilde{x}}{\partial x}\frac{\partial}{\partial \widetilde{x}} = \beta \frac{\partial}{\partial \widetilde{x}} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} = \beta^2 \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \widetilde{x}^2} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0
  & = \left( 1 - M_\infty^2 \right) \varphi_{xx} + \varphi_{yy} + \varphi_{zz} = \\
  & = \left( 1 - M_\infty^2 \right) \beta^2 \varphi_{\widetilde{x} \widetilde{x}} + \varphi_{yy} + \varphi_{zz} = \\
  & = \varphi_{\widetilde{x} \widetilde{x}} + \varphi_{yy} + \varphi_{zz} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
if \(\beta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-M^2_\infty}}\).


\subsubsection{Nature of the equation}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/potential-equation:nature-of-the-equation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Discussion with 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional equation first}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the free\sphinxhyphen{}stream is \sphinxstylestrong{subsonic}, \(M_\infty \in [0,1)\)%
\begin{footnote}[4]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
In order to get a subsonic flow in the whole domain, the free\sphinxhyphen{}stream velocity should be smaller than the speed of sound enough to avoid local supersonic regions in the flow.
%
\end{footnote}, the differential equation is \sphinxstylestrong{elliptic}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the free\sphinxhyphen{}stream is \sphinxstylestrong{supersonic}, \(M_\infty > 1\) (and no shock occurs? Or how to treat them? How strong can they be?) the differential equation is \sphinxstylestrong{hyperbolic}. \sphinxstyleemphasis{Method of characteristics…}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} 3\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional equation


\subsection{Pressure coefficient}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/potential-equation:pressure-coefficient}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pressure coefficient is defined as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}c_p = \frac{p-p_\infty}{\frac{1}{2}\rho_\infty U_\infty^2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Subsonic flow.} Linearizing momentum equation for homoentropic flows,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  h - h_\infty 
  = \frac{U_\infty^2}{2} - \frac{(\mathbf{u}_\infty + \mathbf{u}') \cdot (\mathbf{u}_\infty + \mathbf{u}')}{2}
  \simeq - \mathbf{u}_\infty \cdot \mathbf{u}' \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using \(dh = T ds + \frac{dp}{\rho}\) for homoentropic flows, \(ds = 0\), \(dp = \rho dh\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}p' = p - p_\infty \simeq \rho_\infty ( h' - h_\infty ) = - \rho_\infty \mathbf{u}_\infty \cdot \mathbf{u}' \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that the linearized pressure coefficient reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}c_p = - \frac{2 \mathbf{u}_\infty \cdot \mathbf{u}'}{U_\infty^2} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
With the assumption of \(\mathbf{u}_\infty = U_\infty \hat{\mathbf{x}}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}c_p = - \frac{2}{U_\infty} \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial x} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Now, the pressure coefficient for compressible flow can be compared with the pressure coefficient for incompressible flow \(c_p^{inc}\) in the same domain (e.g. with the same geometry of solid bodies).
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  c_p(x,y,z)
  & = - \frac{2}{U_\infty} \frac{\partial \varphi(x,y,z)}{\partial x} = && \widetilde{\varphi}(\widetilde{x},y,z) = \varphi(x(\widetilde{x}),y,z) \\
  & = - \frac{2}{U_\infty} \frac{\partial \widetilde{x}}{\partial x} \frac{\partial \widetilde{\varphi}(\widetilde{x},y,z)}{\partial \widetilde{x}} = \\
  & = - \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - M^2_{\infty}}} \frac{2}{U_\infty} \frac{\partial \widetilde{\varphi}}{\partial \widetilde{x}}(\widetilde{x},y,z \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}c_p(x,y,z) = \frac{c_p^{inc}(\widetilde{x},y,z)}{\sqrt{1-M_\infty^2}} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\section{Quasi\sphinxhyphen{}1\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional flows}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/quasi-1d:quasi-1-dimensional-flows}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/quasi-1d:compressible-quasi-1d}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/quasi-1d::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Assumptions.} Whenever no explict assumption is made in this section, the following assumptions are made:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
uniform properties on each section of the stream tube

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
negligible viscous and conductivity (non\sphinxhyphen{}ideal flows: friction\sphinxhyphen{}dominated (Fanno), with heat transfer (Rayleigh))

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
