\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
no azimuthal component

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{cylindrical symmetry of streamtube}

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Steady flow}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/quasi-1d:steady-flow}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/quasi-1d:compressible-quasi-1d-steady}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Integral balance equations.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \dfrac{d}{dt} \int_{v_t} \rho + \oint_{\partial v_t} \rho \mathbf{u}^{rel} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = 0 \\
  & \dfrac{d}{dt} \int_{v_t} \rho \mathbf{u} + \oint_{\partial v_t} \rho \mathbf{u} \mathbf{u}^{rel} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \int_{v_t} \rho \mathbf{g}  + \oint_{\partial v_t} \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} \\
  & \dfrac{d}{dt} \int_{v_t} \rho e^t + \oint_{\partial v_t} \rho e^t \mathbf{u}^{rel} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \int_{v_t} \rho \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{u}  + \oint_{\partial v_t} \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{u} - \oint_{\partial v_t} \mathbf{q} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For a control volume \(v_t = V\) at rest, \(\mathbf{u}_b = \mathbf{0}\) and \(\mathbf{u}^{rel} = \mathbf{u}\). Neglecting the volume force \(\mathbf{g} = \mathbf{0}\), and integrating over an elementary control volume \(\Delta V\) cutting a streamtube at coordinates \(z\), \(z + \Delta z\), under steady conditions
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \oint_{\partial \Delta V} \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = 0 \\
  & \oint_{\partial \Delta V} \rho \mathbf{u} \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \oint_{\partial \Delta V} \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} \\
  & \oint_{\partial \Delta V} \rho e^t \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \oint_{\partial \Delta V} \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{u}
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Differential equations.}
Assuming uniform properties on each section,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \dfrac{d}{dz} \left( \rho u A \right) = 0 \\
  & \dfrac{d}{dz} \left( \rho u^2 A + p A \right) - p A' = 0 \\
  & \dfrac{d}{dz} \left[ \rho \left( e^t + \frac{p}{\rho} \right) u A \right] = 0 \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus, momentum equation can be recast as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = \left( \rho u^2 A \right)' + p' A \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Momentum equation}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{0} 
  & = \oint_{\partial \Delta V} \rho \mathbf{u} \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} - \oint_{\partial \Delta V} \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} = \\
  & = \int_{A(z)} \rho \mathbf{u} \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} + p \hat{\mathbf{n}} + \int_{A(z+\Delta z)} \rho \mathbf{u} \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} + p \hat{\mathbf{n}} + \int_{\Delta A^{lat}} p \hat{\mathbf{n}} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional flows,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\hat{\mathbf{z}} \cdot \int_{\Delta A^{lat}} p \hat{\mathbf{n}} = - \Delta z \int_{\ell^{lat}} p \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{z}} \simeq - \Delta z \, p \, \frac{A'(z) \Delta z}{\Delta z} = - p(z) A'(z) \Delta z \ . \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For 3\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional flows,…

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using mass equation, \(( \rho u A )' = 0\), \(\rho u A =: \dot{m}\), momentum and total energy equations become
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \rho u A u' + p' A = 0 \\
  & \rho u A h^{t \, '} = 0 \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or, simplifying momentum equation for the area of the section of the stream\sphinxhyphen{}tube and total energy equation for a mass flux \(\dot{m} \ne 0\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \rho u u' + p' = 0 \\
  & h^{t \, '} = 0 \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection{Mach dependence}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/quasi-1d:mach-dependence}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Subsonic and supersonic flows show different behavior. If the differential equations hold (no shock, homoentropic flow, \(ds = 0\)), pressure derivative is proportional to density derivative through the square of the speed of sound,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}d p = a^2(\rho, \overline{s}) d \rho \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \frac{A'}{A}
  & = \left( M^2 - 1 \right) \frac{u'}{u}         \\
  & = - \frac{ M^2 - 1 }{M^2} \frac{\rho'}{\rho}  \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Details}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0 & = \rho u u' + a^2 \rho' && \text{(momentum)} \\
  0 & = \frac{\rho'}{\rho} + \frac{u'}{u} + \frac{A'}{A} && \text{(mass)} \\
    & = - \frac{u u'}{a^2} + \frac{u'}{u} + \frac{A'}{A} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{velocity}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left( M^2 - 1 \right) \frac{u'}{u} = \frac{A'}{A} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus,
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
in a subsonic   flow \(M < 1\), velocity increases as the section of the stream\sphinxhyphen{}tube decreases

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
in a supersonic flow \(M > 1\), velocity increases as the section of the stream\sphinxhyphen{}tube increases

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{density}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
     \frac{\rho'}{\rho} & = - \frac{u^2}{a^2} \frac{u'}{u} \\
     - \frac{M^2 - 1}{M^2} \frac{\rho'}{\rho} & = - \frac{A'}{A} \\
   \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus,
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
in a subsonic   flow \(M < 1\), density decreases as the section of the stream\sphinxhyphen{}tube decreases

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
in a supersonic flow \(M > 1\), density decreases as the section of the stream\sphinxhyphen{}tube increases

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{pressure}

\sphinxAtStartPar
…

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{temperature}

\sphinxAtStartPar
…

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Unsteady flow}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/quasi-1d:unsteady-flow}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/quasi-1d:compressible-quasi-1d-unsteady}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{For a generic control volume \(v_t\)… It could be useful for mechanical/multi\sphinxhyphen{}field system dynamics…}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Integral equations.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \dfrac{d}{dt} \int_{v_t} \rho + \oint_{\partial v_t} \rho \mathbf{u}^{rel} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = 0 \\
  & \dfrac{d}{dt} \int_{v_t} \rho \mathbf{u} + \oint_{\partial v_t} \rho \mathbf{u} \mathbf{u}^{rel} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \int_{v_t} \rho \mathbf{g}  + \oint_{\partial v_t} \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} \\
  & \dfrac{d}{dt} \int_{v_t} \rho e^t + \oint_{\partial v_t} \rho e^t \mathbf{u}^{rel} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \int_{v_t} \rho \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{u}  + \oint_{\partial v_t} \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{u} - \oint_{\partial v_t} \mathbf{q} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For a control volume \(v_t = V\) at rest, \(\mathbf{u}_b = \mathbf{0}\) and \(\mathbf{u}^{rel} = \mathbf{u}\). Neglecting the volume force \(\mathbf{g} = \mathbf{0}\), and integrating over an elementary control volume \(\Delta V\) cutting a streamtube at coordinates \(z\), \(z + \Delta z\), under steady conditions
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \frac{d}{dt} \int_{\Delta V} \rho + \oint_{\partial \Delta V} \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = 0 \\
  & \frac{d}{dt} \int_{\Delta V} \rho \mathbf{u} + \oint_{\partial \Delta V} \rho \mathbf{u} \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \oint_{\partial \Delta V} \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} \\
  & \frac{d}{dt} \int_{\Delta V} \rho e^t + \oint_{\partial \Delta V} \rho e^t \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \oint_{\partial \Delta V} \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{u}
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Differential equations.}
Assuming uniform properties on each section,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \partial_t \left( \rho A \right) + \partial_z \left( \rho u A \right) = 0 \\
  & \partial_t \left( \rho u A \right) + \partial_z \left[ \left( \rho u^2  + p \right) A \right] - p \partial_z A = 0 \\
  & \partial_t \left( \rho e^t A \right) + \partial_z \left[ \rho \left( e^t + \frac{p}{\rho} \right) u A \right] = 0 \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Assuming here rigid stream\sphinxhyphen{}tube with \sphinxstylestrong{known section \(A(z)\)}, \sphinxstylestrong{constant in time \(\partial_t A(z,t) = 0\)}, the differential equations can be recast as a set of PDE, with primary unknowns \((\rho A, m A, E^t A)\) whose
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
conservative form reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
     \partial_t \begin{bmatrix} \rho A \\ \rho u A \\ \rho e^t A \end{bmatrix} +
     \partial_z \begin{bmatrix} \rho u A \\ \frac{( \rho u A )^2}{\rho A} + p A \\ \frac{ (\rho e^t A + p A) (\rho u A) }{ \rho A }  \end{bmatrix} 
     = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ p \partial_z A \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}
   \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
conservative quasi\sphinxhyphen{}linear form reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
     \partial_t \begin{bmatrix} \rho A \\ \rho u A \\ \rho e^t A \end{bmatrix} +
     \begin{bmatrix}
       \cdot  & 1 & \cdot \\
       - \frac{(\rho u A)^2}{(\rho A)^2} + \partial_{\rho A} (pA) & 2 \frac{\rho u A}{\rho A} + \partial_{\rho u A} (pA) & \partial_{\rho e^t A} (pA) \\
       - \frac{(\rho h^t A)(\rho u A)}{(\rho A)^2} + \partial_{\rho A} (pA) \frac{\rho u A}{\rho A} & \frac{\rho h^t A}{\rho A} + \partial_{\rho u A} ( \rho h^t A ) \frac{\rho u A}{\rho A} & \frac{\rho u A}{\rho A} \left( 1 + \partial_{\rho e^t} ( pA ) \right)
     \end{bmatrix}
     \partial_z \begin{bmatrix} \rho A \\ \rho u A \\ \rho e^t A \end{bmatrix}
     = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ p \partial_z A \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}
   \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
convective form reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
     A \partial_t \rho + A ( \rho \partial_z u + u \partial_z \rho ) = - \rho u \partial_z A \\
     \rho A \partial_t u + \rho A u \partial_z u + A \partial_z p = 0 \\
     \rho A \partial_t e^t + \rho A u \partial_z e^t + A \left( u \partial_z p + p \partial_z u \right) = - p u \partial_z A \ .
   \end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
     \partial_t \rho + \rho \partial_z u + u \partial_z \rho = - \rho u \frac{\partial_z A}{A} \\
     \partial_t u + u \partial_z u + \frac{ \partial_z p }{\rho} = 0 \\
     \partial_t e^t + u \partial_z e^t + \frac{u}{\rho} \partial_z p + \frac{p}{\rho} \partial_z u  = - \frac{p u}{\rho} \frac{\partial_z A}{A} \ .
   \end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{Internal energy equation}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \partial_t e 
  & = \partial_t e^t - \partial_t \frac{u^2}{2} = \\
  & = -u \partial_z e^t - \frac{u}{\rho}\partial_z p - \frac{p}{\rho} \partial_z u - \frac{pu}{\rho} \frac{\partial_z A}{A} + u \partial_z \frac{u^2}{2} + \frac{u}{\rho} \partial_z p = \\
  & = -u \partial_z e - \frac{p}{\rho} \partial_z u - \frac{pu}{\rho} \frac{\partial_z A}{A} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split} \partial_t e + u \partial_z e = - \frac{p}{\rho} \partial_z u - \frac{pu}{\rho} \frac{\partial_z A}{A} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Entropy equation}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  T D_t s 
  & = D_t e - \frac{p}{\rho^2} D_t \rho = \\
  & = - \frac{p}{\rho} \partial_z u - \frac{pu}{\rho} \frac{\partial_z A}{A} - \frac{p}{\rho^2} \left( - \rho \partial_z u - \rho u \frac{\partial_z A}{A}  \right) = \\
  & = 0 \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or, as \(T > 0\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0
  & = D_t s = \\
  & = \partial_t s + u \partial_z s \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{Discuss homoentropic flow, if no shock occurs}
\subsubsection*{Characteristics}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Quasi linear form with mass, momentum and entropy equation and \((\rho, u, s)\) primary variables reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
  \partial_t \begin{bmatrix} \rho \\ u \\ s \end{bmatrix} +
  \begin{bmatrix}
    u & \rho & \cdot \\
    \frac{1}{\rho}\left( \partial_\rho p \right)_s & u & \frac{1}{\rho}\left( \partial_s p \right)_\rho \\
    \cdot & \cdot & u
  \end{bmatrix}
  \partial_z \begin{bmatrix} \rho \\ u \\ s \end{bmatrix} =
  \begin{bmatrix} - \rho u \frac{\partial_z A}{A} \\ 0 \\ 0  \end{bmatrix} \ .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The derivative \((\partial_\rho p)_s = a^2\) is the square of the speed of sound, as its meaning becomes clear in the spectrum of the convection matrix.
These equations looks like 1\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional Euler equations for compressible ideal flows, with the exception that a non\sphinxhyphen{}uniform section of the stream\sphinxhyphen{}tube acts as a source term in mass equation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Spectrum \sphinxhyphen{} eigenvalues.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = |\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{u}) - s \mathbf{I}| = ( u - s )^3 - ( u - s ) a^2 \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}s_{1,3} = u \mp a \quad , \quad s_2 = u \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Right eigenvectors.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\mathbf{R} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
 \rho  & \rho  & \rho  \\
 -a    & \cdot & a     \\
 \cdot & - \frac{\rho a^2}{(\partial_s p)_{\rho}} & \cdot 
\end{bmatrix}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Left eigenvectors.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\mathbf{L} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
 \frac{1}{2 \rho}  & - \frac{1}{2 a}  &  \frac{(\partial_s p)_\rho}{2 \rho a^2}  \\
 \cdot             &           \cdot  & -\frac{(\partial_s p)_\rho}{  \rho a^2}  \\
 \frac{1}{2 \rho}  &   \frac{1}{2 a}  &  \frac{(\partial_s p)_\rho}{2 \rho a^2}  \\
\end{bmatrix}
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxstepscope


\section{Non\sphinxhyphen{}ideal quasi\sphinxhyphen{}1 dimensional flows}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/quasi-1d-non-ideal:non-ideal-quasi-1-dimensional-flows}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/quasi-1d-non-ideal:compressible-quasi-1d-non-ideal}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/quasi-1d-non-ideal::doc}}\subsubsection*{Details}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{3\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional flows.} Equations for a generic volume \(v_t\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \dfrac{d}{dt} \int_{v_t} \rho + \oint_{\partial v_t} \rho \mathbf{u}^{rel} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = 0 \\
  & \dfrac{d}{dt} \int_{v_t} \rho \mathbf{u} + \oint_{\partial v_t} \rho \mathbf{u} \mathbf{u}^{rel} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \int_{v_t} \rho \mathbf{g}  + \oint_{\partial v_t} \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} \\
  & \dfrac{d}{dt} \int_{v_t} \rho e^t + \oint_{\partial v_t} \rho e^t \mathbf{u}^{rel} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \int_{v_t} \rho \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{u}  + \oint_{\partial v_t} \mathbf{t}_{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{u} - \oint_{\partial v_t} \mathbf{q} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} + \int_{v_t} \rho r \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For a volume \(V\) at rest, \(\mathbf{u}^{rel} = \mathbf{u}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Quasi\sphinxhyphen{}1 dimensional approximation.} Introducing the quasi\sphinxhyphen{}1 dimensional model, the contributions of heat conduction through lateral walls and heat source can be collected in one term,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}-\int_{\partial \Delta S^{lat}} \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{q} + \int_{\Delta V} \rho r = \rho r A \Delta z \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
while the conduction along the axis of the stream\sphinxhyphen{}tube reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}-\int_{\partial A(z)} \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{q} - \int_{\partial A(z+\Delta z)} \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{q} \simeq 
A(z) q(z) - A(z+\Delta z) q(z+\Delta z) = - \partial_{z} ( q A ) \Delta z + o(\Delta z) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
With a hydraulic approximation%
\begin{footnote}[1]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
This is a high\sphinxhyphen{}Reynolds model, with viscous stress proportional to dynamic pressure through a friction coefficient and the ration of the area of the section and the hydraulic diameter, \(\frac{A}{D_h}\). As a reference see chapter about {\hyperref[\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/07_similitudine/07teoria:fluid-mechanics-similitude}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Similitude}}}} and in particular the exexricse and the discussion about {\hyperref[\detokenize{polimi/fluidmechanics-ita/template/capitoli/07_similitudine/0706in:fluid-mechanics-similitude-moody}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Moody’s diagram}}}}.
%
\end{footnote}, the contribution of viscous stress in the momentum equation can be written as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\oint_{\partial v_t} \mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{n}} = - \frac{f_d A}{2 D_h} \rho \mathbf{u} |\mathbf{u}|\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Quasi\sphinxhyphen{}1 dimensional model: differential equations.} The conservative form of governing equations of compressible flows with friction and heat coduction reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\partial_t \mathbf{u} + \partial_z \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{u}) + \partial_z \mathbf{F}^d(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{s} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or explicitly
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
  \partial_t \begin{bmatrix} \rho A \\ \rho u A \\ \rho e^t A \end{bmatrix}
+ \partial_z \begin{bmatrix} \rho u A \\ \rho u^2 A + p A \\ \rho u h^t \end{bmatrix}  
+ \partial_z \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ - q A \end{bmatrix}  
= \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ p \partial_z A - \frac{f A}{2 D_h} \rho u |u| \\ \rho r A  \end{bmatrix}  \ ,
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the axial heat conduction is logically serapated from the «convective» flux, as it’s usually a \sphinxstylestrong{diffusive term} containing 2\sphinxhyphen{}nd order spatial derivative of primary variables, and changing the mathematical nature of the equations. As an example, using Fourier’s law, \(q = -k \partial_z T\), this term becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ \partial_z ( k \partial_z T ) \end{bmatrix} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If axial conduction is negligible if compared to convection and heat conduction through the walls of the streamtube, this contribution can be set to zero.

\section{Normal shocks}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/shock-normal:normal-shocks}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/shock-normal:compressible-shocks-normal}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/shock-normal::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Jump conditions.} A normal shock is a discontinuity in the physical quantities of the flow, with non\sphinxhyphen{}zero mass flux \(\dot{m} \ne 0\) across it and zero tangential component of the velocity. {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/jump-conditions:compressible-jump-conditions}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Jump conditions}}}} across a normal shock are
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0 & = [ \dot{m} ] = [ \rho u_{n}^{rel} ]   \\
  \mathbf{u}_\mathbf{t} & = \mathbf{0} \\
  0 & = \dot{m} [ u_n ] + [ \, p \, ] = \dot{m} [ u_n^{rel} ] + [ \, p \, ]  \\ 
  0 & = \dot{m} [ h^{t,rel} ] = \dot{m} [ h^{t,rel}_n ] 
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}



\subsection{Perfect ideal gas}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/shock-normal:perfect-ideal-gas}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/shock-normal:compressible-shocks-normal-pig}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For \DUrole{xref,myst}{perfect ideal gas}, the ratio between quantities before and after normal shocks can be evaluated analitically.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Notation.} Here \(u_n^{rel} = u\) for brevity.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Jump conditions.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
  \rho_1 u_1 = \rho_2 u_2 \\
  \rho_1 u_1^2 + p_1 = \rho_2 u_2^2 + p_2 \\
         \frac{u_1^2}{2} + h_1 =        \frac{u_2^2}{2} + h_2 \\
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

and thus if \(M_1^2 > 1\), then \(M_2^2 < 1\), and viceversa. \sphinxstylestrong{Entropy condition} \(s_2 - s_1 \ge 0\) defines the feasible shocks: \sphinxstylestrong{for a PIG, feasible shocks have \(M_1 > 1\) and \(M_2 < 1\)}, i.e. supersonic flow becomes subsonic after a normal shock.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the function is singular for \(M_1^2 = \frac{\gamma-1}{2\gamma}\). This condition only occurs for \(M_1 < 1\), i.e. it never happens for physical shocks.

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{Entropy condition \sphinxhyphen{} PIG}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \frac{\gamma-1}{R} (s_2 - s_1)
 & = \ln \left\{ \left( \frac{1+ \gamma M_1^2}{1 + \gamma M_2^2} \right)^{1+\gamma} \left( \frac{M_2^2}{M_1^2} \right)^{\gamma} \right\} = \\
 & = \ln \left\{ \left(\frac{ 2 \gamma M_1^2 - \gamma + 1}{\gamma + 1} \right)^{\gamma+1} \left( \frac{2 + ( \gamma - 1 ) M_1^2}{2 \gamma M_1^2 - \gamma + 1}  \right)^{\gamma} M_1^{-2 \gamma} \right\} = \\
 & = \ln \left\{ \frac{ 2 \gamma M_1^2 - \gamma + 1}{(\gamma + 1)^{\gamma+1}} \frac{(2 + ( \gamma - 1 ) M_1^2)^{\gamma}}{M_1^{2 \gamma}} \right\} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Remarks.}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
For \(M_1 = 1\), \(x(M_1) = \{ \dots \}\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\{ \dots \}(M_1=1) = \frac{(\gamma+1) (\gamma+1)^{\gamma+1}}{(\gamma+1)^{\gamma+1}} = 1 \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}s_2 - s_1 \propto \ln \{ \dots \} = 0 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the derivative w.r.t. \(M_1^2\) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
    & \frac{(\gamma+1)^{\gamma+1}}{2 \gamma M_1^2 - \gamma + 1} \frac{2 \gamma}{(\gamma+1)^{\gamma+1}} + \frac{M_1^{2 \gamma}}{(2 + (\gamma-1)M_1^2)^ \gamma } \left( \gamma (2 +(\gamma-1)M_1^2)^{\gamma-1} (\gamma-1) M_1^{-2\gamma} - (\dots) \gamma M_1^{2(\gamma-1)}  \right) = \\
    & = \frac{2 \gamma}{2 \gamma M_1^2 - \gamma + 1} + \frac{\gamma (\gamma-1)}{2 + (\gamma-1) M_1^2} - \frac{\gamma}{M_1^2} = \\
    & = \dots \text{(see below)} =  \\ 
    & = \frac{2 \gamma (\gamma-1) (M_1^2 - 1)^2}{(2 \gamma M_1^2 - \gamma + 1)(2 + (\gamma-1) M_1^2) M_1^2} \ .
  \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The derivative is \sphinxstylestrong{always non\sphinxhyphen{}negative} and thus \sphinxstylestrong{the entropy condition \(s_2 - s_1 \ge 0\) is satisfied only for \(M_1 \ge 1\)}, i.e. for supersonic inflow becoming subsonic (see above) after a normal shock.

\end{itemize}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & 4 \gamma M_1^2 + 2 \gamma (\gamma - 1) M_1^4 + \\
  & \quad + \underbrace{2 \gamma^2 (\gamma-1) M_1^4}_{1} - \underbrace{\gamma (\gamma-1)^2 M_1^2}_{0} + \\
  & \quad - 4 \gamma^2 M_1^2 - \underbrace{2 \gamma^2 ( \gamma - 1 ) M_1^4}_{1} + 2 \gamma ( \gamma - 1 ) + \underbrace{\gamma ( \gamma - 1 )^2 M_1^2}_{0} = \\
  & = 2 \gamma ( \gamma - 1 ) - M_1^2 4 \gamma ( \gamma - 1 ) + 2 \gamma ( \gamma - 1 ) M_1^4 = \\
  & = 2 \gamma ( \gamma - 1 ) ( M_1^2 - 1 )^2 \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsubsection*{Details}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Mach number \(M_2\) can be recast as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}M_2^2 = \frac{2 + (\gamma-1)M_1^2}{2 \gamma M_1^2 - (\gamma-1)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let’s evaluate the ratio of functions of Mach numbers apeparing in ratios of physical quantities
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \frac{1 + \gamma M_1^2}{1 + \gamma M_2^2}
  & = \frac{1 + \gamma M_1^2}{1 + \gamma \frac{2 + (\gamma-1)M_1^2}{2 \gamma M_1^2 - (\gamma-1)}} = \\
  & = \frac{(1+\gamma M_1^2)(2 \gamma M_1^2 - \gamma + 1)}{2 \gamma M_1^2 - \gamma + 1 + 2 \gamma + \gamma ( \gamma - 1 )M_1^2 } = \\
  & = \frac{(1+\gamma M_1^2)(2 \gamma M_1^2 - \gamma + 1)}{\gamma M_1^2 + 1 + \gamma + \gamma^2 M_1^2} = \\
  & = \frac{(1+\gamma M_1^2)(2 \gamma M_1^2 - \gamma + 1)}{( \gamma + 1 ) ( 1 + \gamma M_1^2 )} = \\
  & = \frac{2 \gamma M_1^2 - \gamma + 1}{\gamma + 1} = \\
  & = 1 + \frac{2 \gamma ( M_1^2 - 1 )}{\gamma + 1} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Pressure.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{p_2}{p_1} = 1 + \frac{2 \gamma}{\gamma + 1} ( M_1^2 - 1 )\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Velocity.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \frac{u_2}{u_1}
  & = \frac{M_2^2}{M_1^2} \frac{1+ \gamma M_1^2}{1+\gamma M_2^2} = \\
  & = \frac{2 + (\gamma-1) M_1^2}{(\gamma + 1)M_1^2} = \\
  & = \frac{2 + (\gamma+1) M_1^2 - 2 M_1^2}{(\gamma + 1)M_1^2} = \\
  & = 1 - \frac{2}{\gamma+1}\frac{ M_1^2 - 1 }{M_1^2} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Density.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}
  & = \frac{u_1}{u_2} = \left[ 1 - \frac{2}{\gamma+1}\frac{ M_1^2 - 1 }{M_1^2} \right]^{-1} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Speed of sound.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \frac{a_2^2}{a_1^2} 
  & = \frac{\frac{p_2}{p_1}}{ \frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} } = \\
  & = \left( 1 + \frac{2 \gamma}{\gamma + 1} ( M_1^2 - 1 ) \right) \left( 1 - \frac{2}{\gamma+1}\frac{ M_1^2 - 1 }{M_1^2}  \right) = \\
  & = 1 + \frac{2}{(\gamma+1) M_1^2} \left( \gamma M_1^2 - 1 \right) \left( M_1^2 - 1 \right) + \gamma \left( \frac{2}{\gamma+1} \right)^2 \left( \frac{M_1^2 - 1}{M_1} \right)^2
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Temperature.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{T_2}{T_1} = \frac{a_2^2}{a_1^2}\end{split}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{Oblique shocks}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/shock-oblique:oblique-shocks}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/shock-oblique:compressible-shocks-oblique}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/shock-oblique::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/jump-conditions:compressible-jump-conditions}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{Jump conditions}}}}


\subsection{Normal Component Analysis}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/shock-oblique:normal-component-analysis}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The oblique shock is treated as a normal shock acting only on the normal component of the Mach number:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(M_{n1} = M_1 \sin \beta\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(M_{n2} = M_2 \sin(\beta - \theta)\)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The tangential component of velocity remains preserved: \(u_{t1} = u_{t2}\).


\subsection{The \protect\(\theta\protect\)\sphinxhyphen{}\protect\(\beta\protect\)\sphinxhyphen{}\protect\(M\protect\) Relation}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/shock-oblique:the-theta-beta-m-relation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
By relating the geometry of the velocity vectors (\(\tan \beta = \frac{u_{n1}}{u_t}\) and \(\tan(\beta - \theta) = \frac{u_{n2}}{u_t}\)) and substituting the density ratio \(\rho_2/\rho_1\), we arrive at the «\(\theta\)\sphinxhyphen{}\(\beta\)\sphinxhyphen{}\(M\) equation»:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\tan \theta = 2 \cot \beta \left[ \frac{M_1^2 \sin^2 \beta - 1}{M_1^2 (\gamma + \cos 2\beta) + 2} \right]\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Observations from the \protect\(\theta\protect\)\sphinxhyphen{}\protect\(\beta\protect\)\sphinxhyphen{}\protect\(M\protect\) function}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/shock-oblique:observations-from-the-theta-beta-m-function}}\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Two Solutions:} For any given \(M_1\) and \(\theta < \theta_{max}\), there are two possible shock angles \(\beta\):
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Weak Shock:} Smaller \(\beta\), usually results in \(M_2 > 1\). This is the one typically observed in open flow.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Strong Shock:} Larger \(\beta\), results in \(M_2 < 1\). Usually occurs in confined flows or high back\sphinxhyphen{}pressure.

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Maximum Deflection:} If \(\theta\) exceeds \(\theta_{max}\) for a given \(M_1\), no straight oblique shock solution exists, and the shock becomes \sphinxstylestrong{detached} (bow shock).

\end{enumerate}

\section{Expansion fans \sphinxhyphen{} Prandtl\sphinxhyphen{}Meyer relation}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/prandtl-meyer:expansion-fans-prandtl-meyer-relation}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/prandtl-meyer:compressible-prandtl-meyer}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/prandtl-meyer::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A Prandtl\sphinxhyphen{}Meyer expansion fan is a continuous centering of Mach waves that occurs when a \sphinxstylestrong{supersonic flow} is turned «away» from itself, such as around a convex corner. The flow is homoentropic, and the flow properties (density, pressure, temperature, velocity,…) vary smoothly across the fan while the Mach number increases. The fan connects two regions of the domain with uniform properties.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{todo}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Figure}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Script with Euler solver in 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional domains. To be written, so far only 1\sphinxhyphen{}d solver on GDrive}

\end{itemize}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
Under the assumptions of:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ideal flow \sphinxhyphen{} negligible viscosity and heat conduction

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
no shocks, so that the differential equation holds in the whole domain

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
uniform entropy and zero vorticity at the inflow of the domain

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
the flow in the whole domain is \sphinxstylestrong{homoentropic}, \(s(\mathbf{r}, t) = \overline{s}\), and \sphinxstylestrong{irrotational}, \(\boldsymbol\omega(\mathbf{r},t) = \mathbf{0}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Under the additional assumption of steady flow and uniform conditions at inflow, the flow is \sphinxstylestrong{homo\sphinxhyphen{}total\sphinxhyphen{}enthalpic}, i.e. \(h^t(\mathbf{r}) = \overline{h}^t\).
\subsubsection*{Entropy}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Under the assumptions:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
ideal flow \sphinxhyphen{} negligible viscosity an heat conduction

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
no shock

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
the {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/entropy:compressible-entropy}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{differential entropy equation}}}} becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}D_t s = 0 \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and it governs the evolution of the entropy in the whole domain (as it holds in the whole domain in absence of shocks). Thus, the entropy of any material particle is constant in time. If all the material particles entering the domain have the same entropy, it immediately follows that the entropy is uniform in the whole domain,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}s(\mathbf{r},t) = \overline{s} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Vorticity}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Under ideal flow assumptions \sphinxhyphen{} negligible viscosity and heat conduction \sphinxhyphen{} {\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/vorticity:compressible-vorticity}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{vorticity dynamical equation}}}} reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
  D_t \boldsymbol\omega = \boldsymbol\omega \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u} - \boldsymbol\omega \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} + \frac{1}{\rho^2} \nabla \rho \times \nabla p
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Using mass equation, \(D_t \rho + \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0\), and thus \(-\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} = D_t \rho\). Expressing the pressure field as a function of density and entropy as thermodynamic independent variables, \(p(\rho, s)\), its gradient becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\nabla p = \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_s \nabla \rho + \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial s} \right)_\rho \nabla s \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Under the assumptions of homoentropic flow, \(s(\mathbf{r},t) = \overline{s}\), it follows that \(\nabla s = \mathbf{0}\) and \(\nabla p = a^2(\rho, \overline{s}) \nabla \rho\). Under these assumptions, the term \(\nabla \rho \times \nabla p\) is identically zero.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The vorticity equation becomes (after multiplying by \(\frac{1}{\rho}\), \(\rho \ne 0\)),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \frac{1}{\rho} D_t \boldsymbol\omega = \frac{1}{\rho} \boldsymbol\omega \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u} - \frac{1}{\rho} \boldsymbol\omega \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} \\
  & \frac{1}{\rho} D_t \boldsymbol\omega = \frac{1}{\rho} \boldsymbol\omega \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u} + \frac{1}{\rho^2} \boldsymbol\omega D_t \rho \\
  & \frac{1}{\rho} D_t \boldsymbol\omega - \frac{1}{\rho^2} \boldsymbol\omega D_t \rho  = \frac{1}{\rho} \boldsymbol\omega \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u} \\
  & D_t\left( \frac{ \boldsymbol\omega }{\rho} \right) = \frac{ \boldsymbol\omega }{\rho} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This equation is formally the same as the vorticity equation for incompressible flow with uniform density: here the vector field \(\frac{\boldsymbol\omega}{\rho}\)
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
evolves as a material vector

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
if it’s zero at a point in space and time, it remains equal to zero along the trajectory of the material particle

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
if it’s zero at a set of points where material points enter the domain (inflow), it’s equal to zero on all the trajectories originating from those points. If every trajectory in the domain originates in a irrotational region of the flow, and there’s no shock in the domain so that the differential equation holds, the flow is irrotational in the whole domain.

\end{itemize}
\subsubsection*{Total enthalpy \sphinxhyphen{} steady flow}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The differential form of total energy equation reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho \partial_t e^t + \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla e^t = \rho \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{u} + \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbb{T} \cdot \mathbf{u} \right) - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with the stress tensor of a Newtonian fluid \(\mathbb{T} = - p \mathbb{I} + \mathbb{S}\), and the viscous stress tensor \(\mathbb{S} = 2 \mu \mathbb{D} + \lambda \left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} \right) \mathbb{I}\). For an ideal flow, \(\mathbb{S} = \mathbb{0}\), \(\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}\). If volume force is negligible, \(\mathbf{g}=\mathbf{0}\). Under these assumptions,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \rho \partial_t e^t + \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla e^t
  & = - \nabla \cdot ( p \mathbf{u} ) = \\
  & = - \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla p - p \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} = \\
  & = - \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \frac{ \nabla p }{\rho} - \frac{p}{\rho} \left( - \partial_t \rho - \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \rho \right) = \\
  & = \frac{p}{\rho} \partial_t \rho - \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \left[ \frac{\nabla p}{\rho} - \frac{p}{\rho^2} \nabla \rho \right] = \\ 
  & = \frac{p}{\rho} \partial_t \rho - \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \left( \frac{p}{\rho} \right) \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}-\rho \left[ \partial_t e^t - \frac{p}{\rho^2} \partial_t \rho \right] = \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla h^t \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with the total enthalpy \(h^t = e^t + \frac{p}{\rho}\). Under steady conditons, \(\partial_t \equiv 0\), it follows that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split} \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla h^t = 0 \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e. the total enthalpy is constant on every trajectory. If the physical quantities are uniform at the inflow, total enthalpy is uniform in the whole domain, and not only on every individual trajectory, i.e. the flow is \sphinxstylestrong{homo\sphinxhyphen{}total\sphinxhyphen{}enthalpic}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Under these assumptions, the governing equations of the flow are the homoentropic Euler equations, i.e. in convective form using \(\rho, \mathbf{u}\) as the dynamical variables
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & D_t \rho + \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0 \\
  & \rho D_t \mathbf{u} + a^2(\rho, \overline{s}) \nabla \rho = \mathbf{0} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with the constraint \(s(\mathbf{r}, t) = \overline{s}\), and a constitutive equation to write the speed of sound as a function of the independent thermodynamic variables. As the entropy is uniform, it can be treated as a parameter, so that there’s need for only one independent thermodynamic variable, here \(\rho\). All the other thermodynamic variables can be evaluated a posteriori, once the density field is known as \(f(\mathbf{r},t) = f(\rho(\mathbf{r},t), \overline{s})\), with the notational abuse of using \(f\) for the same physical quantity, but for functions with different arguments.
\label{ch/compressible/prandtl-meyer:example-0}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Example 19.5.1 (Speed of sound \sphinxhyphen{} Perfect ideal gas)}



\sphinxAtStartPar
For a perfect ideal gas,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{p}{\rho} = R T \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and the internal energy is a function of the temperature \(T\) only
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}e = c_v T \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with a constant heat capacity at constant volume \(c_v\). Using the first principle of thermodynamics
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}de = T ds + \frac{p}{\rho^2} d \rho \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
it follows, from Meyer relation and the definition of heat coefficient ratio \(\gamma\) listed below,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  d p 
  & = d \rho R T + \rho R dT = \\
  & = d \rho R T + \rho R \frac{1}{c_v} de = \\
  & = d \rho R T + \rho R \frac{1}{c_v} \left[ T ds + \frac{p}{\rho^2} d \rho \right] = \\
  & = \frac{R}{c_v} \rho T d s + \left[ 1 + \frac{R}{c_v}  \right] R T d \rho = \\
  & = \frac{R}{c_v} \rho T d s + \left[ 1 + \gamma - 1  \right] R T d \rho = \\
  & = \frac{R}{c_v} \rho T d s + \gamma R T d \rho \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that the speed of sound is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}a^2(\rho, s) = \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_s = \gamma R T(\rho, s) = \gamma R \rho^{\gamma-1} e^{\frac{s}{c_v}} \frac{T_0}{\rho_0^{\gamma-1}} e^{-\frac{s_0}{c_v}} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
having used the relations derived below for a perfect ideal gas.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Meyer relation and heat coefficient ratio used above are
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & c_p = c_v + R            && \text{(Meyer relation)}\\
  & \gamma = \frac{c_p}{c_v} && \text{(Heat coefficient ratio)} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned} 
  \frac{c_v}{R} & = \frac{1}{\gamma - 1} \\
  \frac{c_p}{R} & = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma - 1} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dividing the expression of the differential of pressure \(dp(s, \rho)\) by \(p\), and using the equation of state of ideal gas with constant heat coefficients,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{dp}{p} = \frac{1}{c_v} d s + \gamma \frac{d \rho}{\rho} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and after integration w.r.t. a reference state \(0\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \ln \frac{p}{p_0} & = \frac{1}{c_v} \left( s - s_0 \right) + \gamma \ln \frac{\rho}{\rho_0} \\
  \ln \left\{ \left( \frac{p}{p_0} \right) \left( \frac{\rho}{\rho_0} \right)^{-\gamma} \right\} & = \frac{s - s_0}{c_v} \\
  \frac{p \rho^{-\gamma}}{p_0 \rho_0^{-\gamma}} & = e^{ \frac{s-s_0}{c_v} } \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or with \(p = \rho R T\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \frac{T \rho^{1-\gamma}}{T_0 \rho_0^{1-\gamma}} & = e^{ \frac{s-s_0}{c_v} } \\
  \frac{T}{T_0} & = \left(\frac{\rho}{\rho_0}\right)^{\gamma-1} e^{ \frac{s-s_0}{c_v} } \\
  T(\rho, s) & = \rho^{\gamma-1} e^{\frac{s}{c_v}} \frac{T_0}{\rho_0^{\gamma-1}} e^{-\frac{s_0}{c_v}}
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsection{Characteristic lines and compatibility equations}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/prandtl-meyer:characteristic-lines-and-compatibility-equations}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/prandtl-meyer:compressible-prandtl-meyer-characteristics}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Link to \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea/ch/pde/characteristics.html\#euler-equations-for-homoentropic-inviscid-compressible-flows-2d}{Method of characteristics:Homoentropic inviscid compressible flows \sphinxhyphen{} 2d}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A steady expansion fan at a sharp corner connects two regions of the domain with supersonic flow and homogeneous characteristics. Let \(1\) be the inflow homogeneous region and \(2\) the outflow homogeneous region.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In a 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional domain there are three families of characteristic lines. Characteristic lines (or surfaces in 3\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional problems) are defined as those lines orthogonal to the directions \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}_i\) that makes the eigenvalue \(s_i\) of the matrix \(\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{n}}\) equal to zero. The eigenvalues of the matrix \(\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{n}}\) are
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  s_{1,3} & = \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} \mp a \\
  s_{2}   & = \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thus,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \hat{\mathbf{u}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_{1,3} & = \pm \frac{1}{M} \\
  \hat{\mathbf{u}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_{1,3} & = 0 \ . 
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
On characteristic lines the following compatibility equations hold
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \ell_{1,3}: \ 0 & = \frac{\sqrt{M^2-1}}{M^2} \frac{\partial_{\tau} \rho}{\rho} \mp \partial_{\tau} \theta \\
  \ell_{2  }: \ 0 & = \frac{1}{\rho} \partial_{\tau} p + \partial_{\tau} \frac{V^2}{2} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(V = |\mathbf{u}|\). Some characteristic lines of family \(1\) and \(2\) start from inflow homogeneous region and reach outflow homogeneous region. The compatibility equation on characteristic lines of family \(2\) is nothing but the directional derivative of the total enthalpy along streamlines, and thus it’s identically satisfied.
\subsubsection*{\protect\(d h\protect\)}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The differential of enthalpy \(h(p(\rho,s), s)\) reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  d h = T ds + \frac{d p }{\rho}
  & = T ds + \frac{1}{\rho} \left[ (\partial_\rho p)_s d \rho + (\partial_s p)_\rho d s \right] = \\
  & = \frac{a^2}{\rho} d \rho + \left( T + \frac{1}{\rho} (\partial_s p)_\rho \right) ds \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and for homoentropic flows becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}d h = \frac{dp}{\rho} = \frac{a^2}{\rho} d \rho \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(a^2(\rho,s) = \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_s(\rho,s)\) the square of the local speed of sound.
\subsubsection*{Total enthalpy on streamlines, or \protect\(\, \ell_2 \,\protect\) characteristic lines}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If \(h^t(\mathbf{r}) = \overline{h^t}\) uniform, then
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{0} = \nabla h^t = \nabla h + V \nabla V = \left( \partial_\rho h \right)_s \nabla \rho + \left( \partial_s h \right)_\rho \nabla s + V \nabla V \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and for homoentropic flows, \(\nabla s = 0\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{0} = \nabla h^t = \frac{\nabla p}{\rho} + V \nabla V = \frac{a^2}{\rho} \nabla \rho + \nabla \frac{V^2}{2} \ . \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
As the relation \(\Delta h^t = 0\) holds, the compatibility equations on characteristic lines \(\ell_2\) is identically satisfied, being the directional derivative of \(h^t\) along the local direction of the velocity field, \(\partial_{\mathbf{u}} h^t = \hat{\mathbf{u}} \cdot \nabla h^t \equiv 0\).


\subsection{Relation between Mach number and flow deflection}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/prandtl-meyer:relation-between-mach-number-and-flow-deflection}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/prandtl-meyer:compressible-prandtl-meyer-m-theta}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
First the relation between \(d\rho\) and \(d M\) is evalauted in the whole domain of the homo\sphinxhyphen{}total\sphinxhyphen{}enthaplic flow
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0 = d h^t 
  & = dh + V d V = \\
  & = \frac{d p}{\rho} + M a d ( M a ) = \\
  & = a^2\frac{d \rho}{\rho} + M a^2 d M + M^2 a d a = \\
  & = a^2\frac{d \rho}{\rho} + M a^2 d M + \frac{1}{2} M^2 d a^2 = \\
  & = a^2\frac{d \rho}{\rho} + M a^2 d M + \frac{1}{2} M^2 \left( \frac{\partial a^2}{\partial \rho} \right)_s d \rho \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
i.e.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{d \rho}{\rho} = - \frac{M^2}{1 + \frac{1}{2} M^2 \frac{\rho}{a^2} \left( \frac{\partial a^2}{\partial \rho} \right)_s}  \frac{dM}{M} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and then this relation is inserted in the compatibility equation on \(\ell_1\) \sphinxhyphen{} connecting the two uniform regions \sphinxhyphen{} in terms of \(d \rho\), \(d \theta\) to get
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \partial_{\tau_1} \theta
 & = - \frac{\sqrt{M^2-1}}{1 + \frac{1}{2} M^2 \frac{\rho}{a^2} \left( \frac{\partial a^2}{\partial \rho} \right)_s}\frac{\partial_{\tau_1} M}{M} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Details}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \partial_{\tau_1} \theta
 & = \frac{\sqrt{M^2-1}}{M^2} \frac{\partial_{\tau_1} \rho}{\rho} = \\
 & = - \frac{\sqrt{M^2-1}}{M^2} \frac{M^2}{1 + \frac{1}{2} M^2 \frac{\rho}{a^2} \left( \frac{\partial a^2}{\partial \rho} \right)_s}\frac{\partial_{\tau_1} M}{M} = \\
 & = - \frac{\sqrt{M^2-1}}{1 + \frac{1}{2} M^2 \frac{\rho}{a^2} \left( \frac{\partial a^2}{\partial \rho} \right)_s}\frac{\partial_{\tau_1} M}{M} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\label{ch/compressible/prandtl-meyer:example-1}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Example 19.5.2 (Perfect Ideal Gas)}



\sphinxAtStartPar
Equation of state of perfect ideal gas… in a homoentropic flow, \(p \rho^{-\gamma} = p_0 \rho_0^{-\gamma}\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left( \frac{\partial a^2}{\partial \rho} \right)_s = \left( \frac{\partial^2 p}{\partial^2 \rho} \right)_s = \gamma ( \gamma - 1) p_0 \left( \frac{\rho}{\rho_0}  \right)^{\gamma} \rho^{-2} = \gamma ( \gamma - 1 ) p \rho^{-2} \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that the denominator reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}1 + \frac{M^2}{2} \frac{\rho}{\gamma \frac{p}{\rho}} \gamma ( \gamma - 1 ) \frac{p}{\rho^2} = 1 + \frac{\gamma - 1}{2} M^2 \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and the relation between flow deflection and Mach number becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 \partial_{\tau_1} \theta
 & = - \frac{\sqrt{M^2-1}}{1 + \frac{\gamma - 1}{2} M^2}\frac{\partial_{\tau_1} M}{M} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\end{sphinxadmonition}

\chapter{Riemann problem}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/riemann-problem:riemann-problem}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/riemann-problem:compressible-riemann-problem}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/riemann-problem::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Riemann problem is time\sphinxhyphen{}dependent problem, starting from a piecewise\sphinxhyphen{}uniform initial condition.

\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{ch/compressible/riemann-problem-psys:compressible-riemann-problem-psys}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{std,std-ref}{\sphinxstylestrong{P\sphinxhyphen{}sys}}}}}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\section{P\sphinxhyphen{}system}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/riemann-problem-psys:p-system}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/riemann-problem-psys:compressible-riemann-problem-psys}}\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/riemann-problem-psys::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Riemann problem in the P\sphinxhyphen{}sys.} 1\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional P\sphinxhyphen{}sys is a \sphinxstylestrong{two}\sphinxhyphen{}variable hyperbolic system. Riemann problem for the P\sphinxhyphen{}sys aims at finding the \sphinxstylestrong{two} waves (either shock or expansion waves), connecting the uniform regions with conservative variables \(\mathbf{u}_L\), \(\mathbf{u}_R\) on the left and the right of the discontinuity respectively, through \sphinxstylestrong{one} intermediate state \(\mathbf{u}_1\) to be determined as a part of the solution of the Riemann problem.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Depending on the value of the intermediate state \(\mathbf{u}_1\),
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the \sphinxstylestrong{left wave} is
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a rarefaction wave if \(u_L < u_1\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a shock wave if \(u_L > u_1\)

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the \sphinxstylestrong{right wave} is
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a rarefaction wave if \(u_1 < u_R\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a shock wave if \(u_1 > u_R\)

\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For two states connected by a shock wave, Rankine\sphinxhyphen{}Hugoniot relation holds
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left( u_B - u_A \right)_{1,2} = \mp \frac{a} \left( \sqrt{\frac{\rho_B}{\rho_A}} - \sqrt{\frac{\rho_A}{\rho_B}} \right)\ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For two states connected by an expansion wave, the following relation holds
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}(u_B- u_A)_{1,2} = \mp a \ln \frac{\rho_B}{\rho_A} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Entropy condition?} …

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Differential equations.} In conservative form
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\partial_t \begin{bmatrix} \rho \\ m \end{bmatrix} + 
\partial_x \begin{bmatrix} m \\ \frac{m^2}{\rho} + a^2 \rho \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{0} \ ,
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with constant speed of sound \(a\). Convective form reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\partial_t \begin{bmatrix} \rho \\ m \end{bmatrix} + 
\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ a^2 - \frac{m^2}{\rho^2} & 2 \frac{m}{\rho} \end{bmatrix}
\partial_x \begin{bmatrix} \rho \\ m \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{0} 
\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Spectral decomposition \sphinxhyphen{} Characteristics}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Eigenvalues.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}0 = |\mathbf{A} - s \mathbf{I}| = \left| \begin{bmatrix} -s & 1 \\ a^2 - u^2 & -s +2u \end{bmatrix} \right| = s ( s - 2 u ) + u^2 - a^2\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}s_{1,2} = u \mp a\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Right eigenvectors.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{R} = \begin{bmatrix} \rho & \rho \\ \rho ( u - a ) & \rho ( u + a ) \end{bmatrix}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Left eigenvectors.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{L} = \frac{1}{2 \rho^2 a} \begin{bmatrix} \rho ( u + a ) & - \rho \\ - \rho (u-a) & \rho \end{bmatrix}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Spectral decomposition.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{R} \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \mathbf{L} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Characteristic lines and Riemann invariants.} Let \(\mathbf{v}\) the characteristic variables defined by the condition \(d \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{L} d \mathbf{u}\), the PDE
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{0} 
  & = \partial_t \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{u}) \partial_x \mathbf{u} = \\
  & = \partial_t \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{R} \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \mathbf{L} \partial_x \mathbf{u} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
after multiplying by \(\mathbf{L}\) on the left, becomes the diagonal system of equation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\partial_t \mathbf{v} + \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \partial_x \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(\mathbf{V}(t) = \mathbf{v}(X(t),t)\) the value of the characteristic variables on the line \(X(t)\). Exploiting the derivation of composite functions,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}d_t \mathbf{U}(t) = \partial_t \mathbf{u}(X(t),t) + \dot{X}(t) \partial_x \mathbf{u}(X(t), t) \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and inserting in the PDE,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0
  & = \partial_t v_i + s_i \partial_x v_i = \\
  & = d_t V_i + ( s_i - \dot{X} ) \partial_x v_i \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Characteristic lines are defined by the condition \(\dot{X}_i(t) = s_i(\mathbf{U}(t))\), and on these lines \(d_t V_i = 0\), i.e. the \(i^{th}\) characteristic variable is constant on the characteristic lines of the \(i^{th}\) family. For a P\sphinxhyphen{}sys, characteristic lines of family 1, 2 satisfy
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases} \dot{X}_{1,2}(t) = a - u(X_{1,2}(t), t) \\ 0 = \dot{V}_{1,2} = \frac{1}{2 R^2 a} \left[ R (a \pm U) \dot{R} \mp R \dot{M} \right] = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{\dot{R}}{R} \mp \frac{\dot{U}}{a} \right] = \frac{1}{2} \frac{d}{dt} \left[ \ln \left( \frac{R}{\rho_0} \right) \mp \frac{U}{a} \right] \end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(\dot{m} = \dot{\rho} u + \rho \dot{u}\)

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Integral equations.} On a control volume \(V\) at rest
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 & \dfrac{d}{dt} \int_{V} \rho + \oint_{\partial V} \mathbf{m} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = 0 \\
 & \dfrac{d}{dt} \int_{V} \mathbf{m} + \oint_{\partial V} \left[ \frac{\mathbf{m} \mathbf{m}}{\rho} + a^2 \rho \mathbb{I} \right] \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \mathbf{0} \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and for an arbitrary volume \(v_t\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 & \dfrac{d}{dt} \int_{v_t} \rho + \oint_{\partial v_t} \rho ( \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_b ) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = 0 \\
 & \dfrac{d}{dt} \int_{v_t} \rho \mathbf{u} + \oint_{\partial v_t} \rho \mathbf{u} \left( \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_b \right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} + \oint_{\partial v_t} \rho a^2 \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \mathbf{0} 
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Jump conditions.}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
  0 = \left[ \rho u^{rel} \right] \\
  0 = \left[ \rho u u^{rel} + \rho a^2 \right]
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Shocks}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The speed of the shock can be written as a function of the physical quantities on its sides, with \(n\) different expressions, one per component of the relation
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\dot{s} \left[ \mathbf{u} \right] = \left[ \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{u}) \right] \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
here for the P\sphinxhyphen{}sys
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
  \rho_1 ( u_1 - \dot{s} ) = \rho_2 ( u_2 - \dot{s} ) \\
  \rho_1 ( u_1 - \dot{s} ) u_1 + \rho_1 a^2 = \rho_2 ( u_2 - \dot{s} ) u_2 + \rho_2 a^2 
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \dot{s} 
  & = \frac{\rho_2 u_2 - \rho_1 u_1}{\rho_2 - \rho_1} = \\
  & = \frac{\rho_2 ( u_2^2 + a^2 ) - \rho_1 ( u_1^2 + a^2 )}{\rho_2 u_2 - \rho_1 u_1} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Comparing the two expressions of the speed of the shock, a relation between physical quantities on the sides of the shock appears
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  0 
  & = ( \rho_2 u_2 - \rho_1 u_1 )^2 - ( \rho_2 - \rho_1 )( \rho_2 (u_2^2 + a^2 ) - \rho_1 (u_1^2 + a^2 ) ) = \\
  & = \rho_2^2 u_2^2 - 2 \rho_1 \rho_2 u_1 u_2 + \rho_1^2 u_1^2 - \rho_2^2 (u_2^2 + a^2) - \rho_1^2 (u_1^2 + a^2) + \rho_1 \rho_2 ( u_2^2 + 2 a^2 + u_1^2 ) = \\
  & = - 2 \rho_1 \rho_2 u_1 u_2 - \rho_2^2 a^2 - \rho_1^2 a^2 + \rho_1 \rho_2 ( u_2^2 + 2 a^2 + u_1^2 ) = \\
  & = \rho_1 \rho_2 ( u_1 - u_2 )^2 - a^2 ( \rho_2 - \rho_1 )^2 \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus the \sphinxstylestrong{Rankine\sphinxhyphen{}Hugoniot} relation follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\left( u_2 - u_1 \right)_{1,2} = \mp \frac{a}{\sqrt{\rho_1\rho_2}} ( \rho_2 - \rho_1 ) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The speed of the shock is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \dot{s}_{1,2}
  & = \frac{1}{\rho_2 - \rho_1} \left[ \rho_2 \left( u_1 \mp \frac{a}{\sqrt{\rho_1 \rho_2}} (\rho_2 - \rho_1) \right) - \rho_1 u_1 \right] = \\
  & = \frac{1}{\rho_2 - \rho_1} \left[ \left( \rho_2 - \rho_1 \right) u_1 \mp \rho_2 \frac{a}{\sqrt{\rho_1 \rho_2}} (\rho_2 - \rho_1) \right] = \\
  & = u_1 \mp a \sqrt{\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}}
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \dot{s}_{1,2}
  & = \frac{1}{\rho_2 - \rho_1} \left[ \rho_2 u_2 - \rho_1 \left( u_2 \pm \frac{a}{\sqrt{\rho_1 \rho_2}} (\rho_2 - \rho_1) \right) \right] = \\
  & = u_2 \mp a \sqrt{\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_2}}
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Self\sphinxhyphen{}similar solutions at a discontinuity in the initial state.}
\subsubsection*{Self\sphinxhyphen{}similar solution \sphinxhyphen{} expansion fan}

\sphinxAtStartPar
With the similarity variable
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\xi = \frac{x}{t} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and the function \(\mathbf{U}(\xi) = \mathbf{u}(x, t)\),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  \partial_t \mathbf{u} & = \partial_t \xi \mathbf{U}' = - \frac{x}{t^2} \mathbf{U}'(\xi) \\
  \partial_x \mathbf{u} & = \partial_x \xi \mathbf{U}' =   \frac{1}{t  } \mathbf{U}'(\xi) \\
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that the equation becomes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{0} = - \xi \mathbf{U}' + \mathbf{A} \mathbf{U}' = \left[ - \xi \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{A} \right] \mathbf{U}'(\xi) \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This is an eigenvalue problem, as the trivial solution \(\mathbf{U}'(\xi) = \mathbf{0}\) can’t produce a smooth function between two discontinuous states. The solution of the eigenvalue problem reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\xi_{1,2} = U(\xi) \mp a \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with right eigenvectors
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{r}_{1,2} = \begin{bmatrix} \rho(\xi) \\ \rho(\xi) ( u(\xi) \mp a ) \end{bmatrix} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These conditions define two families of expansion fans, one originating from the first family of charactersitic and one originating from the second family.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The derivative of the conservative variable w.r.t. \(\xi\) must be proportional to the right eigenvectors
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{U}'_{1,2}(\xi) = \begin{bmatrix} \rho_{1,2}' \\ m_{1,2}' \end{bmatrix} = C_{1,2} \begin{bmatrix} \rho \\ m \mp \rho a \end{bmatrix} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
or
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
  \rho' = C \rho \\
  m' = C ( m \mp \rho a )
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Integration gives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\rho_{1,2}(\xi) = \rho_A e^{C (\xi-\xi_A)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}m' = C m \mp C \rho_A a e^{C (\xi-\xi_A)}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The solution reads (see below for a very short review of the solution of this kind of ODE)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  m_{1,2}(\xi) 
  & = m_A e^{C \xi} \mp C \rho_A a \xi e^{C ( \xi - \xi_A)} = \\
  & = m_A e^{C (\xi-\xi_A)} \mp C ( \xi - \xi_A ) \, a  \, \rho_{1,2}(\xi)
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(m(\xi) = \rho(\xi) u(\xi)\), then the velocity field is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}u_{1,2}(\xi) = u_A \mp C ( \xi - \xi_A ) \, a \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This expression can be recast as a function of \(u\) and \(\rho\), as \(C(\xi - \xi_A) = \ln \frac{\rho_{1,2}}{\rho_A}\), as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}u_{1,2}(\xi) = u_a \mp a \ln \frac{\rho_{1,2}}{\rho_A} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}\subsubsection*{Solution of the 1\sphinxhyphen{}st order linear non\sphinxhyphen{}homogeneous ODE}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}y'(x) = C y(x) + A e^{Cx}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The solution of the homogeneous
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}y_o(x) = a e^{C x} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
is propoprtional to the forcing. The particular solution of the non\sphinxhyphen{}homogeneous equation has the form
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}y_p(x) = b x e^{C x} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so that its derivative is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}y'_p(x) = b e^{C x} + b C x e^{C x} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Sostitution in the ODE gives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}b e^{C x} + b C x e^{C x} = C \left( b x e^{Cx} \right) + A e^{Cx} \end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and thus \(b = A\). The solution of the non\sphinxhyphen{}homogeneous equation thus reads
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}y(x) = a e^{Cx} + A x e^{Cx} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with the integration constant \(a\) that is determined by a condition (initial, final, or whatever).

\section{Unsteady}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/characteristics:unsteady}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Euler equations
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 0          & = D_t \rho + \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}  \\
 \mathbf{0} & = \rho D_t \mathbf{u} + \nabla p  \\
 0          & = \rho D_t e^t + \nabla \cdot \left( p \mathbf{u} \right)  \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
 0          & =  \partial_t \rho + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \rho + \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}  \\
 \mathbf{0} & =  \partial_t \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u} + \frac{1}{\rho} \nabla p  \\
 0          & =  \partial_t e + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla e + \frac{p}{\rho} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}  \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
with \(p(\rho, e)\). In Cartesian coordinates
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\begin{bmatrix}
 1     & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot \\
 \cdot & 1     & \cdot & \cdot \\
 \cdot & \cdot & 1     & \cdot \\
 \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & 1     \\
\end{bmatrix}
\partial_t \begin{bmatrix} \rho \\ u \\ v \\ e \end{bmatrix} +
\begin{bmatrix}
  u & \rho & \cdot & \cdot \\
  \frac{1}{\rho}\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho}\right)_e & u     & \cdot & \frac{1}{\rho}\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial e}\right)_\rho \\
  \cdot & \cdot & u     & \cdot \\
  \cdot & \frac{p}{\rho} & \cdot & u     \\
\end{bmatrix}
\partial_x \begin{bmatrix} \rho \\ u \\ v \\ e \end{bmatrix} +
\begin{bmatrix}
  v & \cdot & \rho & \cdot \\
  \cdot & v     & \cdot & \cdot \\
  \frac{1}{\rho}\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho}\right)_e & \cdot & v     & \frac{1}{\rho}\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial e}\right)_\rho  \\
  \cdot & \cdot & \frac{p}{\rho} & v     \\
\end{bmatrix}
\partial_y \begin{bmatrix} \rho \\ u \\ v \\ e \end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \ .
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and looking for curves \(\mathbf{R}(t)\), s.t. the equations become ODEs, for the function \(\mathbf{U}(t) = \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{R}(s(t)), t)\). Since
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}d_t \mathbf{U} = \partial_t \mathbf{u} + \frac{d \mathbf{R}}{d s} \frac{d s}{dt} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u} = \partial_t \mathbf{u} + X'(s) \dot{s} \partial_x \mathbf{u} + Y'(s) \dot{s} \partial_y \mathbf{u} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}

Assuming negligible viscosity and conductivity, Navier\sphinxhyphen{}Stokes equations for compressible fluids become Euler equations%
\begin{footnote}[1]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
NS equations are second\sphinxhyphen{}order in space due to the diffusive contributions of viscous stress \(\nabla \cdot \mathbb{T} = \nabla \cdot \left[ 2 \mu \nabla^s \mathbf{u} + \lambda \left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} \right) \mathbb{T} \right]\) for Newtonian fluids in momentum equation and heat conduction flux \(-\nabla \cdot \mathbf{q} = \nabla \cdot \left( k \nabla T \right)\) with Fourier law in total energy equation. Boundary conditions needed for the mathematical problem change as well: while NS equations require no\sphinxhyphen{}slip boundary conditions apply on solid bodies, \(\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}_b\), Euler equations need only no\sphinxhyphen{}penetration boundary conditions \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \mathbf{u}_b \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\).
%
\end{footnote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The conservative form of Navier\sphinxhyphen{}Stokes equations
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{cases}
 \partial_t \rho + \nabla \cdot \left( \rho \mathbf{u} \right) = 0 \\
 \partial_t \left( \rho \mathbf{u} \right) + \nabla \cdot \left( \rho \mathbf{u} \mathbf{u} \right) = \rho \mathbf{g} + \nabla \cdot \mathbb{T} \\
 \partial_t \left( \rho e^t \right) + \nabla \cdot \left( \rho e^t \mathbf{u} \right) = \rho \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{u} + \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbb{T} \cdot \mathbf{u} \right) - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q}
\end{cases}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
need
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
boundary conditions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{constitutive laws} for relating stress tensor \(\mathbb{T}\) and conductive heat flux \(\mathbf{q}\) to \sphinxstyleemphasis{dynamic variables} \(\rho\), \(\mathbf{m} := \rho \mathbf{u}\), \(E^t := \rho e^t\). As a common example, stress tensor for \sphinxstyleemphasis{Newtonian fluids} is the sum of pressure and viscosity stress, and this latter contribution is linear and isotropic w.r.t. first order spatial derivatives of the velocity field%
\begin{footnote}[2]\sphinxAtStartFootnote
\sphinxstylestrong{todo} \sphinxstyleemphasis{discuss isotropic tensors, or link to \sphinxhref{https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea/ch/tensor-algebra-calculus/algebra-isotropic-tensors.html}{Math:Vector and Tensor Algebra and Calculus:Isotropic Tensors}}
%
\end{footnote},
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbb{T} = - p \mathbb{I} + \mathbb{S} = - p \mathbb{I} + 2 \mu \mathbb{D} + \lambda \left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} \right) \mathbb{I} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(p\) the pressure field, \(\mathbb{D} = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \nabla \mathbf{u} + \nabla^T \mathbf{u} \right]\) the deformation velocity tensor and \(\mu\), \(\lambda\) the viscosity coefficients. \sphinxstyleemphasis{Fourier’s law} provides a linear isotropic relation between the conductive heat flux and the temperature gradient
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{q} = - k \nabla T \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{state equations}, for relating thermodynamic variables appearing in constitutive laws with \sphinxstyleemphasis{dynamic variables}. Using constitutive laws for Newtonian fluids and Fourier’s law, there’s a need for state equations relating pressure, temperature and \sphinxhyphen{} if not possible to model as constant \sphinxhyphen{} viscosity coefficients and heat conductivity,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}

   \end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Usually internal energy is used in state equations. Mass density of total energy is defined as the sum of internal energy and kinetic energy
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}e^t = e + \frac{|\mathbf{u}|^2}{2} \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Uniform and steady reference state}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/acoustics:uniform-and-steady-reference-state}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\overline{\rho}, \overline{\mathbf{u}}, \overline{s}\). Time and space derivatives of the reference state are identically zero, thus Euler equations in convective form
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \partial_t \rho + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \rho + \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0 \\
  & \rho \partial_t \mathbf{u} + \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u} + \nabla p = \rho \mathbf{g} \\
  & \partial_t s + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla s = 0
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
are linearized as
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \partial_t \rho' + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \rho' + \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}' = 0 \\
  & \rho \partial_t \mathbf{u}' + \rho \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u}' + \nabla p' = \rho' \mathbf{g} \\
  & \partial_t s' + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla s' = 0
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the entropy is uniform everywhere (also at the boundary, so that no entropy enters from it), its perturbation is identically zero \(s' = 0\), \(s(\mathbf{r},t) = \overline{s}\). Thus, for any thermodynamic variable written as function of density and entropy as the pair of independent variable, e.g. pressure \(p(\rho, s)\), its differential is a function of the differential of the density only, being \(ds = 0\)
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  dp
  & = \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_s d \rho + \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial s} \right)_\rho \underbrace{d s}_{=0} = \\
  & = \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_s d \rho = \\
  & = c^2(\rho, s) \, d\rho \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Now, for negligible volume forces \(\mathbf{g} = \mathbf{0}\), and writing \(\nabla p = c^2 \nabla \rho\), mass and momentum linearized equations read
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \partial_t \rho' + \overline{\mathbf{u}} \cdot \nabla \rho' + \overline{\rho} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}' = 0 \\
  & \overline{\rho} \partial_t \mathbf{u}' + \overline{\rho} \overline{\mathbf{u}} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u}' + c^2(\overline{\rho}, \overline{s}) \nabla \rho' = \mathbf{0} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & D^{\overline{\mathbf{u}}}_t \rho' + \overline{\rho} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}' = 0 \\
  & \overline{\rho} D^{\overline{\mathbf{u}}}_t \mathbf{u}' + \overline{c}^2 \nabla \rho' = \mathbf{0} \ .
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(D^{\overline{\mathbf{u}}}_t\) the material time derivative with the reference velocity field,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}D^{\overline{\mathbf{u}}}_t = \partial_t + \overline{\mathbf{u}} \cdot \nabla \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}

\subsection{Wave equations}
\label{\detokenize{ch/compressible/acoustics:wave-equations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A wave equation for density perturbation \(\rho'(\mathbf{r},t)\) is obtained taking the difference of time derivative of the mass equation and the divergence of momentum equation,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & D^{\overline{\mathbf{u}}}_{tt} \rho' + \overline{\rho} D^{\overline{\mathbf{u}}}_{t} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}' = 0 \\
  & \overline{\rho} \nabla \cdot D^{\overline{\mathbf{u}}}_t \mathbf{u}' + \overline{c}^2 \nabla^2 \rho' = 0 \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
it follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{1}{\overline{c}^2} D^{\overline{\mathbf{u}}}_{tt} \rho'- \nabla^2 \rho' = 0 \ .\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A wave equation for velocity perturbation \(\mathbf{u}'(\mathbf{r},t)\) is obtained taking the difference of time gradient of the mass equation and the time derivative of momentum equation,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\begin{aligned}
  & \nabla D^{\overline{\mathbf{u}}}_{t} \rho' + \overline{\rho} \nabla \left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}' \right) = 0 \\
  & \overline{\rho} D^{\overline{\mathbf{u}}}_{tt} \mathbf{u}' + \overline{c}^2 D^{\overline{\mathbf{u}}}_{t} \nabla  \rho' = \mathbf{0} \ ,
\end{aligned}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
and using vector identity \(\nabla^2 \mathbf{v} = \nabla \left( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} \right) - \nabla \times \nabla \times \mathbf{v}\), it follows
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\frac{1}{\overline{c}^2} D^{\overline{\mathbf{u}}}_{tt} \mathbf{u}' - \nabla^2 \mathbf{u}' - \nabla \times \boldsymbol\omega' = \mathbf{0} \ ,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
being \(\boldsymbol\omega' = \nabla \times \mathbf{u}'\) the vorticity of the velocity perturbation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For isentropic flows, differential of density perturbation \(d \rho'\) can be related to differential of pressure perturbation, \(d \rho' = \frac{1}{\overline{c}^2} dp'\), so that pressure perturbation field is governed by a wave equation as well.
